sections.title: Start here
sections.body_html:
This book explains how to read the Speak Up sound picture for any English sound. It is written for speech-language pathologists. You do not need an acoustics background; each section starts with what you will see, then explains why, then gives numbers with their sources.

Every number has a citation. Anything that could not be confirmed with the publisher, PubMed or PMC, Crossref or Semantic Scholar is marked UNVERIFIED. Treat those as rough guides.

sections.title: How to use this book
sections.body_html:
Three ways in

  • The index on the left lists every section. Click a title to jump to it.
  • The search bar finds words in titles, keywords and text. Try “gliding”, “F3”, “burst” or “lisp”.
  • For this word. When you open the book from a word page, the sounds of that word are listed at the top and their sections are highlighted. Every other section is still there, so you can look up the sound you think the child actually made and compare.

How each sound entry is laid out

Every sound entry uses the same parts, so you can skip to the one you need:

  1. What it should look like on the spectrogram.
  2. Why these frequencies: what the lips, tongue, jaw and soft palate are doing, and how that moves the formants.
  3. Typical values, children and adults, with ages and sources.
  4. What errors look like and their usual causes.
  5. How to tell it from the sounds it is most often confused with, with links.
  6. On the Speak Up screen: what the app can and cannot show for this sound.

Ground rules

  1. You decide. Arti’s answer and every number on the screen are aids to listening, not a diagnosis.
  2. Age and dialect first. A sound that seems wrong may be expected for the child’s age, or normal in the child’s dialect or home language. See Development and Dialect and second language.
  3. Compare the child with the child. Children’s formants depend on age, size and the word. The most useful comparison is usually the same child’s good token against the same child’s error token. See Compare the child with themselves.

sections.title: Quick look-up: what am I seeing?
sections.body_html:
What you see on the picture Most likely Read
White across all heights Silence, a pause or a stop closure Stops
Thin dark line very low (under about 300 to 500 Hz) during a gap Voicing during a closure (voice bar) Voicing
One thin vertical line top to bottom A stop burst Stops
Speckled noise, no stripes, strongest high up A fricative such as /s/ or /ʃ/ Fricatives
Faint even grey noise A weak fricative /f θ/, or /h/ /f/, /θ/
Dark horizontal bands with fine vertical stripes A vowel or approximant; the bands are formants Vowels
Bands that slide up or down The tongue and lips moving between sounds Transitions
Strong low bar, pale above, sharp edges A nasal /m n ŋ/ Nasals
Red F3 dots dipping down toward green F2 An r sound /r/
F2 very low, F3 high /w/ or a glided r /w/, Gliding
F2 very high, close to F3, F3 also high /i/ or /j/, not r /j/

sections.title: What the research means for Speak Up
sections.body_html:
Six points from the research behind this book matter most when you read Speak Up results.

  1. Some r errors are normal until about 6 to 8. Pooled US data put /ɹ/ at 5;0 to 5;11 at a 90% criterion (Crowe and McLeod 2020). ASHA’s table gives gliding as usually gone by 6 to 7. See Development of r.
  2. Correct r means F3 pulled down toward F2. A good r lowers F3 to roughly 60 to 80% of the speaker’s own vowel F3 (Hagiwara 1995, as reported by later papers). That is why the app looks at the gap between F3 and F2. See /r/.
  3. The gap number is weak on its own for young children. In 3 to 4 year olds, an automatic F3-F2 gap explained only about 37% of listener ratings (Ancel et al. 2023).
  4. Compare a child with themselves. Norms come from small regional samples and from “bird” only (Campbell et al. 2018).
  5. Children’s /s/ is very high. Its energy often peaks at 7 to 9.5 kHz (Todd et al. 2011). Speak Up now records at 48 kHz and the full view shows up to 11 kHz, so the peak is usually visible there; the compact picture stops at 6 kHz and cannot show it. See /s/.
  6. Automatic scoring drops outside the lab. Published r classifiers trained on the same corpus as Arti reach about .81 (F1) in the lab and less in clinical use, and none were tested on 4 to 6 year olds. See Arti’s limits.

sections.title: Reading the screen
sections.body_html: This part explains every strip and tool on the Speak Up analysis page: what it is computed from, what it shows, and when not to trust it. Start with the map of the screen, then read the strip you are looking at.

sections.title: Map of the screen
sections.body_html:
Part of the screen What it is computed from Key settings
Waveform The recorded samples Recorded at 48 kHz, mono
Spectrogram Short-time Fourier transform 6 ms Hann window, 2 ms step, pre-emphasis 0.95, top 50 dB shown, dark means energy. Compact picture 0 to 6 kHz; full view up to 11 kHz
Formant dots Linear prediction (LPC) on a 16 kHz copy Order 14, 25 ms frames every 5 ms, Viterbi tracker; F1 blue, F2 green, F3 red; voiced frames only
Pitch (F0) Normalized autocorrelation on the 16 kHz copy 75 to 500 Hz, 40 ms frames
Intensity Frame loudness (RMS) dB relative to full scale
Spectrum at the cursor One column of the spectrogram Top 50 dB of that column
Target window The part of the word where the target sound should be Shaded on the picture; the F3-F2 gap for r is searched here
Tools Move, Cursor, Scrub, and overlays (Layers, Target sound, Hz ranges, Lines) One pointer tool at a time; overlays on or off

Why a 16 kHz copy for the dots and pitch: formant analysis needs at least 16 kHz, and children’s F4 likely reaches 5 kHz or more (Milenkovic et al. 2020). The picture uses the full 48 kHz recording so high fricative noise can be seen.

sections.title: The waveform
sections.body_html:
The waveform is the recording itself: air pressure at the microphone plotted against time.

  • Voiced stretches (vowels, approximants, nasals) repeat once per vocal fold cycle. At a child’s 270 Hz each repeat lasts about 3.7 ms.
  • Noise (fricatives, aspiration, bursts) looks like dense, irregular fuzz with no repeating pattern. /s/ is fine and dense; /h/ is weaker.
  • Silence is a flat line, or a thin band of room noise.
  • Height shows loudness, but it depends on microphone distance and gain, not just the child.
  • Clipping: if the recording was too loud, the peaks are cut flat at the top and bottom edges. Clipping adds false high-frequency energy and spoils formant and pitch readings. Re-record at lower gain or greater distance rather than interpret it.

Use it first. The waveform is the fastest check of a take: look for flat-topped peaks, a tiny signal (noise will dominate), and where the word starts and ends.

sections.title: The spectrogram
sections.body_html:
A spectrogram is a row of short spectra laid side by side.

  • Left to right is time.
  • Bottom to top is frequency (pitch height of the energy, in Hz).
  • Darkness is energy at that time and frequency. Darker means more.

Speak Up shows the top 50 dB of the recording. Anything more than 50 dB below the loudest point is white. A quiet sound in a loud recording can disappear into white, and a noisy room fills the background with light grey.

What the dark bands are. In a vowel, dark horizontal bands are the formants: the resonances of the throat and mouth (see Source and filter). F1 is the lowest band, then F2, then F3. They move when the tongue, lips or jaw move. The fine vertical stripes inside them are single vocal fold pulses.

Pre-emphasis. Voiced speech loses energy as frequency rises, so F3 and F4 would look pale. A simple filter, y[n] = x[n] - 0.95 x[n-1], boosts high frequencies so F3, the key formant for r, shows clearly. It also makes high noise (fricatives, hiss) look stronger, which is expected.

sections.title: Wideband view and children's voices
sections.body_html:
Every spectrogram trades time detail against frequency detail, set by the length of the analysis window.

  • A short window (a few ms) gives sharp timing and blurs harmonics together, so formants appear as dark bands and each vocal fold pulse as a vertical stripe. This is a wideband spectrogram.
  • A long window (tens of ms) resolves single harmonics as thin horizontal lines. This is narrowband, the right view for intonation, not formants.

The Praat manual gives the classic values: a 5 ms window gives a broadband view with about 260 Hz bandwidth; a 30 ms window gives a narrowband view with about 43 Hz (Praat manual, Sound: To Spectrogram). Speak Up uses a 6 ms Hann window, about 240 Hz bandwidth (from the Hann window’s 1.44-bin width, Harris 1978), close to Praat’s broadband setting.

Why it matters more for children. An adult man at 120 Hz has an 8.3 ms vocal fold period, so 6 ms catches about one pulse at a time. A child at 250 to 300 Hz has a period of only 3.3 to 4 ms. When the child’s pitch gets near the window bandwidth, neighbouring harmonics start to separate even in the wideband view, so you may see faint horizontal striping inside a formant band. It is not a recording fault. With a 2 ms step there are fewer than two columns per period, so the vertical stripes in a child’s vowel may fade. Faint stripes do not mean the vowel is voiceless.

sections.title: Frequency range: 6 kHz and 11 kHz views
sections.body_html:
Speak Up records at 48 kHz, so the recording holds sound up to 24 kHz. Two pictures use it differently:

  • The compact picture (word page) and the 0 to 6 kHz button show 0 to 6 kHz. This covers F1 to F3 and usually F4 in children, the range for vowels, approximants and r.
  • Show all in the full analysis view shows up to 11 kHz when the recording has it. Use it for fricatives: children’s /s/ often peaks at 7 to 9.5 kHz (Todd et al. 2011), so its peak is above the compact picture.

Formants, pitch and Arti always use a 16 kHz copy, which holds nothing above 8 kHz. That is enough for formants (Milenkovic et al. 2020) but not for children’s /s/: listeners needed about 9 kHz of bandwidth to perceive /s/ well from female and child talkers (Stelmachowicz et al. 2001).

sections.title: Formant dots (F1, F2, F3)
sections.body_html:
The coloured dots are the app’s estimate of the formants in each 25 ms frame, every 5 ms: F1 blue, F2 green, F3 red. They appear on voiced frames only.

How they are found. Linear prediction (LPC) fits a smooth curve with a few peaks to each frame; the peaks become formant candidates, and a tracker picks which is F1, F2 and F3 by choosing the smoothest path over time. Speak Up uses order 14, matching the value Milenkovic et al. (2020) give for 5-year-olds at 16 kHz (11 tract coefficients plus 3 to 4 for the source). Praat expresses the same idea as a formant ceiling: about 5000 Hz for men, 5500 Hz for women and up to 8000 Hz for young children (Praat manual, Sound: To Formant). Analysing a child with an adult setting makes the tracker split or invent formants.

Allowed ranges. F1 200 to 1300 Hz, F2 700 to 3800 Hz, F3 1400 to 5000 Hz. They are wide on purpose, so a 4-year-old’s high formants and an older child’s strongly lowered r F3 both fit.

Dots are estimates, the bands are the evidence. If a dot sits in a pale gap, distrust it. See When the dots are wrong.

Dots in places they do not belong. During a nasal murmur, a voice bar or a voiced fricative, the dots follow nasal or low resonances, not vowel formants.

sections.title: When the dots are wrong
sections.body_html:
Children’s high voices space the harmonics 250 to 400 Hz apart, so each formant is outlined by only a few points. The error of formant estimation grows with F0 (Vorperian and Kent 2007), and formant errors “may be unavoidable” above about 200 Hz F0 (Cialdella et al. 2020). Even in carefully hand-checked adult and 10 to 12 year old data, F4 could not be measured in 12 to 17% of tokens (Hillenbrand et al. 1995).

Error What it looks like What is usually happening
Merged formants One colour disappears, or two sit on top of each other Two formants too close to separate (F1 and F2 in /u o/; F2 and F3 in r)
Swap Red drops onto the green band and green onto blue, or the reverse The tracker missed one formant and moved the next one down into its slot
Missed F3 Red dots missing or scattered while a band is still visible F3 weak, or outside 1400 to 5000 Hz
Jump A track leaps hundreds of Hz for a frame or two A noise peak or a harmonic won for those frames
Harmonic locking A track moves in steps, or in parallel with the pitch LPC fitting single harmonics of a high voice

Three checks. (1) Do the dots sit on dark bands? (2) Is the track smooth? Real articulators move smoothly; a 500 Hz leap for one frame is an error. (3) Is the order right? F1 is below F2 is below F3, and in a neutral child vowel they are roughly 1.2 to 1.6 kHz apart.

For r, the key question is whether red F3 truly follows a lowered band toward F2, or has jumped onto F2. Check the spectrum at the cursor: two peaks close together support a real low F3; one peak suggests a merge.

sections.title: Pitch (F0)
sections.body_html:
F0 is how fast the vocal folds vibrate; listeners hear it as pitch. Speak Up measures it by comparing each 40 ms frame with shifted copies of itself (autocorrelation, the method family of Praat’s default, Boersma 1993). A 40 ms frame holds three periods of the 75 Hz floor, the rule the Praat manual gives.

Group Mean F0 (Hz) Source
Men 131 Hillenbrand et al. 1995, all vowels
Women 220 Same
Boys 10 to 12 236 Same
Girls 10 to 12 238 Same
Ages 4 to 12 about 240 to 280, ranges about 200 to 330 Maturo et al. 2012, per-age values from a secondary sheet, UNVERIFIED against the paper’s table

Before puberty boys and girls have nearly the same F0; differences begin around 11 (Lee et al. 1999).

Octave errors. The tracker can jump to exactly half or double the true pitch for a few frames, most often in creaky or breathy voice and at voice onsets. A child reading 130 Hz in the middle of 260 Hz speech has not dropped an octave. Praat has octave costs to discourage this (Praat manual, Sound: To Pitch (ac)).

Uses. The pitch line marks voiced frames (a quick voicing check). A pitch in the adult range suggests an adult voice in the clip. Do not use it to measure VOT: trackers need a few cycles before reporting voice, so they start late.

sections.title: Intensity
sections.body_html:
The intensity line is each frame’s loudness in dB relative to the largest value the recording can hold (0 dBFS); real values are negative.

It shows: relative loudness within one recording, where the syllables are (each vowel is a hump), silent closures (dips), and whether the take is too quiet or too hot.

It does not show: the child’s real loudness. Doubling mouth-to-microphone distance lowers the level by about 6 dB, so moving the device changes the line without any change in the voice. Do not compare intensity between sessions unless distance and gain were held the same.

sections.title: Spectrum at the cursor
sections.body_html:
The small graph below the picture is one moment’s spectrum: frequency left to right, level up and down. It is one column of the spectrogram at the cursor, showing the top 50 dB of that column.

  • Broad peaks are formant candidates. The lowest broad peak in a vowel is usually F1, the next F2.
  • Deep valleys can mean antiresonances: nasals and /l/.
  • Strong high energy with no low peaks means noise (a fricative or burst).
  • With a high-pitched child you may see a small ripple at the harmonic spacing on top of the curve; the formant is the broad hump, not each ripple.

Use it to check the tracker. When F2 and F3 come close (a good r), two distinct peaks a few hundred Hz apart support a real low F3; one broad peak suggests a merge. Move along a few frames to see whether the pattern holds.

Use it for noise. Place the cursor on a burst or a fricative: rising toward the top suggests /t s/, one mid peak suggests /k ʃ/, flat and weak suggests /p f θ/.

sections.title: The target window and the F3-F2 gap
sections.body_html:
The shaded box marks the part of the word where the target sound should be, based on its position in the word (start, middle or end). Today it is used for r: the app searches it for the narrowest F3-F2 gap, using strong frames only. The readout labels this experimental.

How to read the gap. A smaller gap means F3 is closer to F2, which means more r-like. The research measures at the lowest point of F3 inside the r (Campbell et al. 2018; Harel et al. 2017; McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012). Place a cursor there yourself and compare.

Two traps.

  1. /i/ and /j/ also have narrow gaps, because their F2 is very high, not because F3 is low. Confirm that F3 itself dips. See /j/.
  2. The window is a guess from position. If the word was cut wrongly, or the child paused, the window may miss the r. Look at the picture, not just the number.

sections.title: The measures table and frame listing
sections.body_html:
Below the picture, the analysis page lists measures for the selected word.

  • Recording check: length, where the word was found, loudest sample, how much of the clip is speech, and clipped samples. Check these before anything else. Clipped samples or very little speech mean the numbers below are unreliable.
  • Voice: F0 median, lowest and highest, range and spread, and the share of voiced frames. An F0 in the adult range suggests an adult voice. “Adult-voice adjustment” shows when the app rescaled an adult recording.
  • Target sound: for r, the F3-F2 median over the word, the narrowest gap in the target window (experimental), F1 to F3 at that moment, and how many frames had all three formants. Few frames means the result rests on little evidence.
  • Frame listing: every analysis frame’s time and values, for checking a single moment.

sections.title: Recording, the word box and Listen
sections.body_html:
How a recording ends. Speak Up keeps listening until there has been about 2 seconds with no voice, or until you press Stop. The longest recording is 30 seconds. Stop keeps everything recorded so far.

The word box. After a try, the app picks the target word in the recording and draws a box over it on the waveform, labelled “Picked automatically, listen to check”. For a single word it takes the longest voiced stretch (short gaps under about 250 ms are joined). For a phrase or sentence it splits the voiced stretches and takes the one at the target word’s place in the line.

Check it. Press Listen to hear only what is inside the box. If it is the wrong part:

  • drag the left or right edge to grow or shrink that side,
  • drag the middle to slide the whole box,

like cropping a photo. The label changes to “Moved by you”. When you let go, Arti scores the new box, and the analysis page shows only the boxed word.

Why it matters. Everything on the analysis page, and Arti’s answer, describes only the box. A box that includes your own voice, a second word, or noise gives misleading numbers.

sections.title: The toolbar
sections.body_html:
The tools above the picture come in two kinds.

  • Pointer tools decide what a click or drag on the picture does. Only one is active at a time: Move (the default), Cursor and Scrub.
  • Overlay tools add information on top of the picture. Each turns on and off by itself: Layers, Target sound, Hz ranges and Lines.

The zoom buttons and Play what is shown stay in the toolbar whatever tool is active. The help line under the picture changes with the active pointer tool.

sections.title: Move tool and zoom
sections.body_html:
Move is the default. Drag to slide the picture left and right; the mouse wheel zooms time; Shift and the wheel zoom frequency. Double-click shows everything. No crosshair follows the mouse.

Zoom buttons: Zoom in, Zoom out, Show all (up to 11 kHz when the recording has it), 0 to 6 kHz, and Zoom to the target window.

Play what is shown plays exactly the stretch of time on screen. Zoom to a single sound and play it to hear what you are looking at.

sections.title: Cursor tool
sections.body_html:
Cursor lets you place markers that stay where you put them.

  • Lines option: “Time only” draws a vertical line (a moment in time); “Time and Hz” adds a horizontal line (a frequency) as well.
  • Click the picture to place a cursor. It stays; the mouse does not drag a crosshair afterwards.
  • Add cursor arms the next click to place another cursor, with the Lines choice shown at that moment. Up to six cursors, each a different colour and numbered 1 to 6 on the picture and in the readout.
  • Drag a cursor to move it. Press Delete, or the x in the readout, to remove it.

The readout lists each cursor’s time, its Hz (if it has a Hz line), F1 to F3 at that frame, and the time between cursors 1 and 2.

Good uses. Put cursor 1 at a burst and cursor 2 at the first voice pulse to read VOT (VOT). Put one cursor at the F3 minimum of r and another in the vowel to compare F3 (Compare the child with themselves). Measure a fricative or closure duration between two cursors.

sections.title: Scrub tool
sections.body_html:
Scrub lets you hear the sound under the mouse as you drag. Drag right and it plays forward at the speed you drag: slowly for a slow drag. Drag left and it plays backwards. A still mouse is silent.

Use it to find exactly where a sound starts and ends, for example where the r turns into the vowel, or whether a short /s/ is there before a /t/. Then check whether Arti and the target window are looking at the right moment.

sections.title: Layers
sections.body_html: Layers turns each formant’s dots (F1, F2, F3) and the target window shading on and off. Hide the dots to look at the bare spectrogram bands, which are the better evidence when the tracker struggles (When the dots are wrong).

sections.title: Target sound highlight
sections.body_html: Target sound emphasises the formants that carry the target sound inside the target window. For r these are F2 and F3, and the gap between them is shaded: a correct r brings F3 down toward F2 (/r/). For other sounds the key formants are listed in each sound entry under “On the Speak Up screen”. Turning it off removes the highlight.

sections.title: Hz ranges
sections.body_html:
Hz ranges shows where the target sound’s formants usually fall for a child of this age, from published studies.

  • Bands: faint shaded stripes behind the key formants, at the published range for the child’s age.
  • Numbers: the same ranges in the readout, with the source.
  • Both (default): bands and numbers.

When no checked study covers the child’s age and sound, it says “No reliable range for this age” instead of guessing. The app does not know the child’s sex, so where studies split boys and girls the ranges are merged and labelled “boys and girls together”.

Read the band as “where most children’s values sit”, never as a pass or fail line. Published child samples are small and regional, and the spread is wide in young children (for r, standard deviations up to about 500 Hz at ages 5 to 8 in Flipsen et al. 2001). A value outside the band is a reason to listen again, not a finding. See Norms and their limits.

sections.title: Lines: joining the formant dots
sections.body_html:
Lines changes how each formant’s dots are drawn, so you can see the shape of the movement:

  • Dots: the raw estimates.
  • Straight lines: dots joined in order.
  • Smoothed: a smooth curve through the dots.
  • Lines and dots: both.

Lines are never drawn across a gap of more than 3 missing frames, so a break means the tracker found no formant there. Smoothing makes a shape easier to see but can hide a real fast movement, such as the quick F3 dip of an onset r; check with Dots when in doubt.

sections.title: Recognising sound classes at a glance
sections.body_html:
What you see What it is
White across all heights Silence: a pause, a stop closure, or before the word
Thin dark band at the very bottom during a gap Voice bar: voicing during a closure, as in /b d g/
A thin vertical spike spanning many heights A stop burst (/p t k b d g/ release)
Grainy noise with no stripes or bands, often strongest high up Frication (/s ʃ f θ/)
Dark horizontal bands with vertical stripes A vowel or approximant (/r l w j/)
Bands that glide up or down Formant transitions: the articulators moving
Strong low band, weak above, abrupt edges A nasal murmur (/m n ŋ/)

Children’s nasal murmurs and formants sit higher than adults’ for the same tract-length reason (Children are not small adults).

sections.title: Before you read anything: a checklist
sections.body_html:
1. Waveform: no flat-topped clipping; the word is well above the background.
  2. Word box: it covers the target word and nothing else; Listen to check.
  3. Spectrogram: background mostly white, the word clearly visible, bands visible in the vowels.
  4. Pitch: plausible for a child (roughly 200 to 330 Hz); no isolated jumps to half or double.
  5. Formant dots: on dark bands, smooth, in the right order.
  6. Spectrum at the cursor: peaks agree with the dots at the moment you care about.
  7. Compare: against the same child’s own better tokens, recorded the same way.

sections.title: How the mouth shapes the sound
sections.body_html:
Every pattern on the spectrogram comes from two things: a sound source (the vocal folds, or air hissing through a narrow gap) and the shape of the throat and mouth, which acts as a filter. Moving the jaw, tongue, lips or soft palate changes that shape, and the formants move in predictable directions. This part explains those directions, so you can look at a formant pattern and picture what the mouth did.

Movement Main effect on the picture
Jaw opens, tongue lowers F1 rises (Jaw and tongue height)
Tongue body moves forward F2 rises (Front and back)
Lips round or protrude All formants fall, F2 most clearly (Lips)
Narrowing at the palate, the throat and the lips together F3 falls a long way: the r pattern (Constrictions and F3)
Closure at the lips, tongue tip or tongue back F2 and F3 bend toward a place-specific start (Place of articulation)
Soft palate lowers Nasal resonance and antiresonances added; vowels dull (Nasal coupling)
Narrow gap with fast airflow Noise, shaped by the space in front of the gap (Noise sources)

sections.title: Source and filter
sections.body_html:
The standard account of speech acoustics (Fant 1960; Stevens 1998) splits each sound into a source and a filter.

  • Voiced source. The vocal folds open and close, chopping the airflow into pulses. A pulse train repeating every T seconds has energy only at F0 = 1/T and its whole-number multiples, the harmonics. On the picture these make the vertical stripes (wideband) or thin horizontal lines (narrowband).
  • Noise source. Turbulent air through a narrow gap (/s ʃ f/) or the sudden release of pressure (a stop burst) makes random energy spread over many frequencies, with no harmonics.
  • Filter. The air in the tube from vocal folds to lips has natural resonances, the formants. Source energy near a resonance passes strongly; energy between resonances is weakened.

The key consequence: the source sets the pitch; the filter sets which vowel or consonant you hear. They are independent. A child and an adult can say the same vowel at very different pitches, and the formants describe the mouth shape, not the pitch. The harmonics only sample the formant curve, which is why high voices are harder to measure (When the dots are wrong).

The commonly quoted slopes (source about -12 dB per octave, lip radiation about +6 dB per octave, net about -6 dB per octave) are textbook idealisations; UNVERIFIED against the books themselves, and real voices differ.

sections.title: The vocal tract as a tube
sections.body_html:
A neutral vowel (schwa) behaves like a tube closed at the vocal folds and open at the lips. Such a tube resonates at odd quarter wavelengths:

Fn = (2n - 1) c / (4L), with c about 35,000 cm/s (warm moist air) and L the tract length.

For a textbook adult male tract of 17.5 cm: F1 = 500, F2 = 1500, F3 = 2500, F4 = 3500 Hz, spaced 1000 Hz apart.

Tract length Example F1 F2 F3 Spacing
17.5 cm Textbook adult male 500 1500 2500 1000
15.0 cm About adult female 583 1750 2917 1167
11.28 cm MRI, boy aged 4;4 (Vorperian and Kent 2007) 776 2327 3879 1551

(Values computed from the formula, not measured.)

Every formant scales with 1/L, so a shorter tract shifts all formants up. This is the single most important fact about children’s speech acoustics: a young child’s neutral F3 sits near 3.9 kHz where an adult man’s is near 2.5 kHz. Never compare a child’s raw values with adult numbers. Real vowels and real children depart from this simple tube (the throat and mouth grow at different rates, Vorperian et al. 2009), so the tube gives the scale, not exact values.

sections.title: Jaw and tongue height: F1
sections.body_html:
Rule: the more open the mouth (jaw lower, tongue lower), the higher F1. High (close) vowels /i u/ have the lowest F1; low (open) vowels /æ ɑ/ the highest.

Why. For a close vowel the tongue makes a narrow constriction in the mouth and leaves the throat wide; that lowers F1. Opening the jaw and lowering the tongue widens the mouth and narrows the throat, which raises F1. Stevens and House (1955) built their classic description of vowels on exactly three numbers: where the tongue constriction is, how narrow it is, and the size of the lip opening. Lindblom and Sundberg (1971) showed with an articulatory model that the jaw works together with the tongue to set vowel openness, and that “tongue height” is best thought of as the result of tongue and jaw together.

Child example (Hillenbrand et al. 1995, boys and girls 10 to 12): F1 about 450 Hz in /i/ (“heed”) against about 1000 Hz in /ɑ/ (“hod”).

Clinical use. A vowel with F1 too high for the target suggests a jaw that is too open or a tongue too low; too low suggests the reverse. A jaw that does not move between syllables gives a flat F1.

sections.title: Tongue front and back: F2
sections.body_html:
Rule: the further forward the tongue body, the higher F2. Front vowels /i ɪ eɪ ɛ æ/ have high F2, close to F3. Back vowels /u ʊ oʊ ɔ ɑ/ have low F2, close to F1.

Why. Moving the tongue forward shortens the space in front of the constriction and enlarges the space behind it, which raises F2. Moving it back does the opposite. /j/ is an even more fronted /i/, so its F2 is very high; /w/ adds a back tongue to rounded lips, so its F2 is very low.

Child example (Hillenbrand et al. 1995, 10 to 12): F2 about 3100 Hz in /i/ against about 1400 Hz in /u/.

Clinical use. F2 too high for a back vowel (for example /u/ said with spread lips and a forward tongue) means fronting; too low for a front vowel means backing.

sections.title: The lips: rounding lowers the formants
sections.body_html:
Rule: rounding or protruding the lips lowers all the formants, F2 most clearly.

Why. Rounding narrows the lip opening and lengthens the tube. In perturbation terms (see Constrictions and F3), the lips are a place where every formant is lowered by narrowing. Lindblom and Sundberg (1971) treat the lips as one of their independent parameters for this reason.

How big. Rounding alone lowers F3 only modestly: in Hillenbrand’s men, /u/ F3 is about 2355 Hz against about 3005 Hz for /i/. It never brings F3 down to r levels (about 1700 Hz in the same men’s /ɝ/). That is why a child who rounds the lips without the r tongue shape sounds like /w/.

Other sounds. Rounding lowers fricative noise too: /s/ before a rounded vowel, or after /w/, has a lower peak (about 4.4 to 4.8 kHz labialised against 5.7 to 6.3 kHz otherwise in adolescents, Koenig et al. 2013 as quoted by Wong and Munson 2025). /ʃ/ is normally said with rounded lips, which helps keep it lower than /s/.

sections.title: Constrictions and F3: why r is special
sections.body_html:
Perturbation theory (Chiba and Kajiyama 1941, developed by Fant and others) says: narrowing the tube where a formant’s air movement is largest (a velocity maximum) lowers that formant; narrowing where its pressure is largest raises it. Each formant has its own pattern of these points along the tract.

  • The lips are a velocity maximum for every formant, so rounding lowers all of them.
  • For F3, the velocity maxima in a quarter-wave tube fall at the lips, the palate and the throat. Narrowing all three at once lowers F3 three times over (Hagiwara 1995; Ohala 1985, as summarised by Espy-Wilson et al. 2000). A typical American r does exactly that: lip rounding, a palatal constriction (tongue tip up or tongue body bunched), and a throat constriction from tongue-root retraction.

What MRI added. Espy-Wilson et al. (2000), modelling real tract shapes, found that perturbation theory alone does not fully explain r and that F3 is mainly a resonance of the space in front of the palatal constriction plus the lips; the space under the tongue enlarges it and gives the lowest F3 values. Story and Bunton (2010) showed more generally that the tract has regions where a constriction pushes each formant in a predictable direction, and that listeners’ place boundaries line up with where F2 or F3 changes direction.

Many tongue shapes, one result. Very different tongue shapes give essentially the same F1 to F3 for r (Delattre and Freeman 1968; Zhou et al. 2008). Retroflex and bunched r differ mainly in F4 and F5. So the spectrogram cannot tell you which shape a child used, and either shape can be correct.

sections.title: Place of articulation: transitions and the F2 locus
sections.body_html:
When the mouth closes or narrows for a consonant and opens into a vowel, the formants slide between the two shapes. These formant transitions are one of the best clues to where the consonant was made.

  • F1 always rises out of a closure (and falls into one), whatever the place, because a closed or narrow tube has a low first resonance.
  • F2 points toward a place-specific start, the locus. With synthetic speech, Delattre, Liberman and Cooper (1955) found loci of about 720 Hz for /b/ and 1800 Hz for /d/ (adult values). For /g/ a locus appeared only before vowels with F2 above about 1200 Hz.
  • Lips (/p b m/): F2 rises into most vowels (it starts low).
  • Tongue tip (/t d n/): F2 starts near the alveolar locus, so it falls into back vowels and stays nearly flat into front vowels.
  • Tongue back (/k g ŋ/): F2 and F3 start close together (the velar pinch), then separate into the vowel.

Locus equations. Sussman, McCaffrey and Matthews (1991) plotted F2 at vowel onset against F2 at vowel middle across many vowels; the slope and intercept of the line separate places (labials steep, alveolars flatter, velars between and often split by vowel). Exact slopes are UNVERIFIED here.

Bursts. The burst spectrum also reflects place: labials weak and flat or falling, alveolars rising toward high frequencies, velars one compact mid peak (Stevens and Blumstein 1978). Kewley-Port (1983) showed that the changes over the first 40 ms, not a single snapshot, identify place well (88% correct by judges).

Coarticulation. Öhman (1966) showed that in vowel-consonant-vowel sequences the consonant rides on a continuous vowel-to-vowel movement, so a consonant’s transitions change with the vowels around it. Children’s loci and bursts are higher than adults’ because their tracts are shorter.

sections.title: The soft palate: nasal coupling
sections.body_html:
When the soft palate (velum) lowers, the nasal cavity joins the tube.

  • Nasal consonants (/m n ŋ/): the mouth is closed and sound leaves through the nose. The long, soft, absorbent nasal tube gives a strong low nasal formant and weak energy above. The closed mouth is a side branch that traps energy at its own resonance, creating an antiformant (zero), a frequency where energy is cancelled. Fujimura (1962) showed that the location of the antiformant is what distinguishes /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/: a longer closed mouth (/m/) gives a lower zero, a shorter one (/n/, then /ŋ/) a higher zero.
  • Nasalized vowels: an extra resonance and antiresonance near F1 flatten and widen the F1 peak and add a low nasal peak. Hawkins and Stevens (1985) produced nasality by adding a pole and zero near F1 and proposed that the basic cue is how prominent the spectral peak near F1 is. Chen (1997) measured this as A1-P0 (F1 amplitude minus nasal peak amplitude), which drops by about 6 to 8 dB for nasalized vowels. Kataoka et al. (1996) found hypernasal vowels had more energy between F1 and F2 and less in the F2 to F3 region.

On a child’s picture these cues are hard to read: the nasal peak and F1 can coincide in low vowels and high voices (Styler 2017), and the 6 ms window smears the detail. Speak Up is not a nasality measure.

sections.title: Noise sources: fricatives and bursts
sections.body_html:
Noise is made where air is forced through a narrow gap fast enough to become turbulent, or where a closure is suddenly released.

Rule: the noise is shaped mainly by the space in front of the gap. The smaller that space, the higher the noise.

  • /s z/: tongue tip or blade at the ridge behind the teeth, a very small front space, and the air jet hits the teeth. Loud, high noise.
  • /ʃ ʒ/: the gap is further back and the lips round, both making the front space larger. Loud noise with a lower peak, roughly 2.5 to 4.5 kHz in adults and higher in children.
  • /f v θ ð/: the gap is at the lips or teeth, leaving almost no front space to shape the noise. Weak, flat noise with no clear peak (Jongman et al. 2000).
  • /h/: noise made at the vocal folds is shaped by the whole tract, so it shows the next vowel’s formants faintly.

Sibilants (/s z ʃ ʒ/) are much louder than non-sibilants because the jet strikes the teeth. Bursts follow the same front-space logic (see Place of articulation).

sections.title: Voicing: voice bars, VOT and vowel length
sections.body_html:
English voiced and voiceless consonants differ in several cues at once.

Voice onset time (VOT) is the time from a stop’s burst to the first vocal fold pulse (Lisker and Abramson 1964).

Category VOT Example adult means (Lisker and Abramson 1964, via Kim 2021)
/p t k/ stressed, word start Long lag: about 40 to 100+ ms, with aspiration noise /p/ 58, /t/ 70, /k/ 80 ms
/b d g/ word start Short lag: about 0 to 25 ms; some speakers prevoice (negative VOT) /b/ 1, /d/ 5, /g/ 21 ms
/p t k/ after /s/ (“spot”) Short lag, unaspirated Like /b d g/

VOT lengthens from lips to tongue tip to tongue back, and is longer before sonorants and high vowels (Klatt 1975).

Children. Macken and Barton (1980) found three stages from about 1;6: no contrast, then a contrast too small for adults to hear (both categories in the short-lag range), then adult-like long lag. Koenig (2000) found 5-year-olds’ voicing control was the most variable of all groups, and argued that VOT development reflects growing control of voicing itself, not only timing. Whiteside and Marshall (2001) still found age and sex changes in VOT between 7 and 11.

Voice bar. Voiced stops and fricatives may keep the vocal folds going during the closure, which shows as a thin dark band at the very bottom of the picture with pitch marks. English /b d g/ often lack it at word start.

Vowel length before final consonants. Vowels are longer before voiced final consonants (“bead” longer than “beat”; Peterson and Lehiste 1960), and listeners use that length to hear the final consonant as voiced or voiceless (Raphael 1972). Final voiced sounds are often partly devoiced in normal speech, so vowel length is often the main cue.

Fricatives. Voiced fricatives have voicing through more of the noise and larger F1 transitions next to them (Stevens et al. 1992).

sections.title: Children are not small adults
sections.body_html:
Children differ from adults in three ways that affect every number on the screen:

  1. Higher formants, because the tract is shorter. It grows from about 6 to 8 cm at birth to about 15 cm in women and 18 cm in men (Vorperian and Kent 2007; Vorperian et al. 2009). Male and female tracts start to differ around puberty (Fitch and Giedd 1999; about age 12 in Vorperian et al. 2009).
  2. Higher F0, about 240 to 280 Hz in school-age children (Pitch).
  3. More variability, between children and within one child. Lee, Potamianos and Narayanan (1999), 436 children aged 5 to 17, found durations reach adult-like consistency around 12, and formant and F0 consistency 2 to 3 years later. Kent (1976) concluded that motor control reaches adult-like accuracy at about 11 or 12, after speech sounds are usually judged mastered.

Scaling is not uniform. Kent and Forner (1979) found that the factor relating children’s to adults’ formants varies somewhat by formant and vowel. In Hillenbrand et al. (1995), 10 to 12 year olds’ formants were 10 to 30% higher than men’s.

Normalization. To compare speakers you must remove size. Options: z-scores across each speaker’s vowels (Lobanov 1971; works well with many vowels per speaker, Adank et al. 2004); ratios or differences between formants in the same frame (for example F3-F2 for r); or comparing the child with themselves. Nearey (1989) reviews why both the token’s own formants and the speaker’s whole vowel system help listeners. For clinical use, comparing the child with themselves is the most robust.

sections.title: Coarticulation: sounds overlap
sections.body_html:
Sounds are not made one at a time. The tongue and lips are already moving toward the next sound while the current one is made.

  • Vowels shift with the consonants around them. Hillenbrand, Clark and Nearey (2001) found large effects of consonant context on vowel formants, especially rounded vowels next to alveolar consonants (F2 pulled up).
  • Consonants shift with the vowels. A consonant’s transitions and burst depend on the vowel (Place of articulation); /s/ before a rounded vowel is lower.
  • The r gesture spreads. The F3 movement for r keeps a similar duration across neighbouring consonants (Boyce and Espy-Wilson 1997), so r can colour the vowels next to it.
  • Children coarticulate more. Nittrouer, Studdert-Kennedy and McGowan (1989), ages 3 to 7 and adults: the /s/-/ʃ/ difference grew with age while the influence of the following vowel on the fricative shrank. Young children seem to plan speech in syllable-sized chunks.

Clinical use. Judge a sound in the same word or context across tries, and expect “the same” sound to look different in “tree” and “red”.

sections.title: Sound by sound
sections.body_html:
One entry for each English sound class and each sound. Every entry has the same parts: what it should look like, why, typical values, errors, how to tell it from look-alikes, and what Speak Up can show.

Vowels: overview. Approximants (/r w l j/): overview. Stops: overview. Fricatives and /h/: overview. Affricates: overview. Nasals: overview.

sections.title: Vowels
sections.body_html:
What vowels look like

Steady, dark horizontal formant bands with vertical voicing stripes and high intensity. F1 is lowest, then F2, then F3. F1 tells you height (open vowels high F1), F2 tells you front or back (front vowels high F2), and lip rounding lowers both F2 and F3 (How the mouth shapes the sound).

  • Front vowels /i ɪ eɪ ɛ æ/: F2 high, close to F3.
  • Back rounded vowels /u ʊ oʊ ɔ/: F2 low, close to F1, with a wide empty space between F2 and F3.
  • Central vowels /ʌ ə/: formants near the neutral-tube spacing.
  • R-coloured vowels /ɝ ɚ/: F3 pulled down near F2. See /r/.

Where the numbers come from

Child values are from Hillenbrand et al. (1995): 27 boys and 19 girls aged 10 to 12 saying /hVd/ words (heed, hid, …), computed from the published data files, plus Peterson and Barney (1952), 15 children of unstated age (UNVERIFIED age range, often described as school age). There is no checked per-age table for ages 4 to 9. Lee et al. (1999) have one but its raw values were not accessed (UNVERIFIED). Treat 5 to 9 year olds as at least as high as the 10 to 12 values, usually higher. Vowels also change during the vowel (“inherent spectral change”, Assmann and Katz 2000), so one moment does not capture a vowel completely.

Mean F0 for these children was about 227 to 247 Hz. Adult values are in each vowel’s entry.

Errors that apply to every vowel

  • Centralised vowel: F1 and F2 pulled toward the middle of the chart (for a child roughly F1 650 to 750 Hz, F2 1500 to 1700 Hz).
  • Fronting or backing: F2 too high or too low for the target.
  • Height errors: F1 too high (jaw too open) or too low.
  • Unwanted r-colouring: F3 drops toward 2000 to 2300 Hz in a child vowel that should have F3 near 3000 Hz.

Non-r vowel errors are less common than consonant errors and are a feature to note in motor speech disorders (Motor speech signs).

On the Speak Up screen

For a 5 to 12 year old expect F1 about 350 to 1050 Hz and F2 about 1100 to 3200 Hz, with F3 about 2900 to 3800 Hz in non-r vowels. With F0 near 250 Hz the dots can lock onto harmonics, and F1 can merge with F0 in /i u/. Check dots against the bands.

sections.title: /i/ as in "heed", "bee"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low F1 and very high F2 close to a high F3. The widest F1-to-F2 distance of any vowel.

Why these frequencies

The tongue body is high and forward: a narrow constriction at the hard palate (low F1) and a short front space with a big throat (high F2). Lips spread.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 444 3028 3602 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 464 3159 3806 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children (age unstated) 360 3178 3763 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 343 2323 3005 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 437 2761 3378 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Lowered F2 (backing or centralising toward /ɪ/ or /ə/); raised F1 (jaw too open, toward /eɪ/ or /ɪ/).

How to tell it from

  • /ɪ/: higher F1 and lower F2, shorter.
  • /j/: even lower F1 and higher F2, but brief and gliding into the next vowel.
  • /r/: /i/ has a narrow F3-F2 gap too (boys about 575 Hz, girls about 650 Hz) because F2 is high, not because F3 is low. In r, F3 itself is low.

On the Speak Up screen

F2 near 3 kHz and F3 near 3.6 to 3.8 kHz in a child sit well inside the 0 to 6 kHz view. F1 in a high-pitched child can sit close to F0 and be missed. In words like “tree” or “reed”, do not let the narrow gap of /i/ count as r.

sections.title: /ɪ/ as in "hid", "sit"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Like /i/ but with F1 a little higher and F2 a little lower, and shorter.

Why these frequencies

The tongue is high and front but less so than /i/, and less tense.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 518 2498 3335 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 506 2640 3513 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 534 2744 3604 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 429 2034 2687 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 484 2369 3057 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Tensing to /i/ (F2 higher, F1 lower, longer) or centralising to /ə/ (F2 lower).

How to tell it from

/i/: lower F1, higher F2. /ɛ/: higher F1. /ə/: lower F2, very short.

On the Speak Up screen

In “rabbit” and “rocket” the /ɪ/ is unstressed and short; expect fewer frames and values drifting toward /ə/.

sections.title: /eɪ/ as in "hayed", "rain"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Mid F1 and high F2, with a small glide upward in F2 and downward in F1 toward /ɪ/ at the end. In American English it is usually a short diphthong.

Why these frequencies

Tongue mid-high and front, moving slightly higher.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 563 2608 3282 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 567 2707 3387 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Men 476 2090 2688 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 535 2526 3045 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

(Values are averages over the vowel; Peterson and Barney did not include this vowel.)

What errors look like

No glide (a flat /e/), or lowering toward /ɛ/.

How to tell it from

/ɛ/: higher F1, no upward glide. /ɪ/: lower F1.

On the Speak Up screen

In “rain” the /eɪ/ follows r; the F3 rise out of the r runs into the vowel, so read the vowel’s values after F3 has levelled off.

sections.title: /ɛ/ as in "head", "bed"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

F1 mid-high, F2 fairly high.

Why these frequencies

Tongue mid and front, jaw more open than for /eɪ/.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 727 2225 3228 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 758 2355 3395 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 700 2616 3564 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 588 1803 2604 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 727 2063 2953 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Raised to /eɪ/ or /ɪ/ (F1 lower), lowered to /æ/.

How to tell it from

/æ/: usually higher F1 (but see the regional note there). /eɪ/: lower F1 and a glide.

On the Speak Up screen

In “carrot”, “very” and “bear” the /ɛ/ is next to r, so F3 falls during the vowel. That is r-colouring from the r, not a vowel error.

sections.title: /æ/ as in "had", "cat"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

High F1 and fairly high F2.

Why these frequencies

Jaw open, tongue low and front.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 704 2472 3186 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 738 2532 3417 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 1017 2334 3366 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 591 1930 2595 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 676 2335 2971 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

Regional note. In the Hillenbrand speakers, /æ/ has a lower F1 than /ɛ/, the reverse of Peterson and Barney. Many American dialects raise /æ/; the Hillenbrand speakers’ region is commonly described as the upper Midwest (UNVERIFIED detail). Judge /æ/ against the child’s dialect.

What errors look like

Raised toward /ɛ/; backed toward /ɑ/ (F2 lower).

How to tell it from

/ɛ/: compare within the child. /ɑ/: much lower F2.

On the Speak Up screen

In “rabbit” the /æ/ follows r: F3 rises out of the r into the /æ/.

sections.title: /ɑ/ as in "hod", "car"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

The highest F1 of any vowel, with F2 low and fairly close to F1.

Why these frequencies

Jaw wide open, tongue low and back, throat narrowed.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 959 1647 2882 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 1039 1740 3015 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 1030 1383 3188 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 756 1309 2535 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 921 1524 2832 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Raised (F1 lower) toward /ʌ/; rounded toward /ɔ/ (F2 lower).

How to tell it from

/ɔ/: lower F1 and F2, rounded. In many American dialects /ɑ/ and /ɔ/ have merged (“cot” and “caught” sound the same); that is not an error. /ʌ/: lower F1.

On the Speak Up screen

F1 near 1 kHz in a child sits close to the top of the F1 tracking range (1300 Hz); a very open child /ɑ/ can lose its F1 dots. In “car” the end of the /ɑ/ should show F3 falling toward F2: that fall is the r (/r/).

sections.title: /ɔ/ as in "hawed", "door"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

F1 fairly high, F2 low and close to F1.

Why these frequencies

Tongue back and low-mid, lips somewhat rounded (lowering F2).

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 794 1249 2873 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 897 1383 3067 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 694 1064 3263 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 656 1023 2521 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 804 1188 2824 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Unrounding (F2 rises toward /ɑ/), raising toward /oʊ/.

How to tell it from

/ɑ/ (may be merged in the child’s dialect), /oʊ/: lower F1.

On the Speak Up screen

F1 and F2 can be within a few hundred Hz and merge in the dots. In “door” the vowel before r is often closer to /o/ and ends with the F3 fall of the r.

sections.title: /oʊ/ as in "hoed", "boat"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Mid F1, low F2 close to F1, with a glide toward /ʊ/ (F1 and F2 both falling slightly).

Why these frequencies

Tongue back and mid, lips rounded, moving higher and more rounded.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 606 1137 2935 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 589 1145 3106 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Men 498 910 2459 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 555 1036 2828 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Unrounded (F2 higher), no glide.

How to tell it from

/ɔ/: higher F1. /u/: lower F1.

On the Speak Up screen

F1 and F2 close together: watch for merged dots.

sections.title: /ʊ/ as in "hood", "book"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low-mid F1, F2 low to mid.

Why these frequencies

Tongue high-mid and back but less than /u/, lips somewhat rounded.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 567 1451 2998 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 575 1583 3187 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 560 1402 3332 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 469 1123 2435 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 519 1229 2829 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Tensed to /u/, or centralised to /ʌ/.

How to tell it from

/u/: lower F1. /ʌ/: higher F1.

On the Speak Up screen

A vocalic r error is sometimes heard as an [ʊ] offglide (“car” ending like “cah-oo”): F2 falls but F3 stays high (Vocalic r errors).

sections.title: /u/ as in "who'd", "blue"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low F1, low F2, wide empty space between F2 and F3.

Why these frequencies

Tongue high and back, lips rounded and protruded: all formants lowered, F2 most.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 493 1325 2938 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 492 1510 3052 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 432 1193 3250 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 380 992 2355 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 460 1106 2735 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

Context. /u/ after alveolar consonants (“two”, “do”) has a much higher F2 than in isolation (Hillenbrand et al. 2001). Many American speakers front /u/ in general.

What errors look like

Spread lips: F2 rises well above the child’s usual /u/.

How to tell it from

/w/: even lower F1 and F2, brief, gliding into a vowel. /ʊ/: higher F1.

On the Speak Up screen

F1 can merge with F0 in a high voice; F1 and F2 can merge in the dots.

sections.title: /ʌ/ as in "hud", "truck"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Mid F1, mid F2: close to the neutral-tube pattern.

Why these frequencies

Tongue mid and central, lips neutral.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Boys 10 to 12 714 1484 3067 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Girls 10 to 12 772 1614 3210 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Children 855 1592 3328 Peterson and Barney 1952
Men 621 1181 2548 Hillenbrand et al. 1995
Women 760 1416 2901 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

What errors look like

Mostly a substitution target: a non-rhotic “bird” sounds like [bʌd] with F3 staying high.

How to tell it from

/ɝ/: similar F1 and F2 but F3 far lower in /ɝ/ (boys 2077 against 3067 Hz). /ə/: shorter, unstressed. /ɑ/: higher F1.

On the Speak Up screen

In “truck” the /ʌ/ follows /tɹ/: look at the start of the vowel for the end of the r’s F3 dip.

sections.title: /ə/ (schwa) as in "about", "carrot"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Very short, weak, with formants near the neutral-tube spacing and strongly pulled toward the neighbouring consonants.

Why these frequencies

A relaxed, central tongue: the tract is close to a uniform tube (The vocal tract as a tube). Being unstressed, it is short and shaped by its neighbours.

Typical values

No checked child table. From the tube formula, a 4-year-old’s tract of about 11.3 cm predicts about 780, 2330 and 3880 Hz; real schwa varies widely with context (values computed, not measured).

What errors look like

Deleted entirely in weak syllable deletion (“nana” for “banana”): one fewer vowel hump in the intensity line (Weak syllable deletion).

How to tell it from

/ʌ/: longer, stressed. /ɚ/: F3 low.

On the Speak Up screen

Few frames; dots may be sparse. Count syllables with the intensity line.

sections.title: Diphthongs /aɪ aʊ ɔɪ/
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

The formants glide from one vowel position to another instead of holding steady. Follow F1 and F2 across the vowel; a diphthong shows a clear slope over 100 ms or more.

Diphthong Example F1 F2
/aɪ/ buy falls (open to close) rises (back to front)
/aʊ/ how falls falls (to back rounded)
/ɔɪ/ boy falls slightly rises a long way
/eɪ/, /oʊ/ hay, hoe small fall small rise (/eɪ/), small fall (/oʊ/)

Why these frequencies

The endpoints follow the vowel rules: opening raises F1, fronting raises F2, rounding lowers F2.

Typical values

Use the endpoint vowels in the vowel table. A developmental study of children’s diphthongs exists (Lee, Potamianos and Narayanan 2014) but its values were not extracted (UNVERIFIED).

What errors look like

A flat track instead of a glide (monophthongisation), or a glide that falls short. Some dialects normally monophthongise /aɪ/ (for example many Southern US speakers), so check dialect first.

On the Speak Up screen

Use Lines (Smoothed) to see the slope. R-coloured endings (“car”, “four”, “air”, “ear”) end in an F3 fall: see /r/.

sections.title: Approximants: /r w l j/
sections.body_html:
Approximants are vowel-like consonants: voiced, with formant bands, made with a narrowing that is not tight enough to make noise. They are told apart mainly by F2 and F3, and by how fast the formants move.

The one-line rule: /r/ has low F3; /w/ has very low F2; /l/ has high F3 and an abrupt edge; /j/ has very high F2. See Telling /r w l j/ apart.

sections.title: /r/ (ɹ, ɝ, ɚ)
sections.body_html:
The core rule: a correct American English r pulls F3 far down toward F2. Most of what follows elaborates that.

What it should look like

  • F3 is unusually low, often low enough to seem to merge with F2. McAllister Byun and Hitchcock (2012) call lowered F3 “the hallmark of American English /r/”. F3 bends down into the r and back up into the next vowel, forming a dip.
  • F2 is moderate to fairly high, not very low as in /w/.
  • F1 is fairly low in consonant r.
  • Onset r (“red”, “rabbit”): a short F3 dip at the start, rising into the vowel.
  • R vowels /ɝ/ (“bird”) and /ɚ/ (“butter”): a longer stretch with F3 held low and F2 and F3 close together.
  • Postvocalic r (“car”, “door”, “bear”): F3 falls toward the end of the vowel.

Why these frequencies

  1. Three narrowings. Typical r narrows the tract at the palate (tongue tip raised in “retroflex” r, or tongue body raised in “bunched” r), in the throat (tongue root pulled back), and usually at the lips (McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012; Zhou et al. 2008).
  2. Each one lowers F3. For F3, these are the three places where narrowing lowers the formant (Constrictions and F3). Lip rounding alone lowers F3 only a little, which is why a child who rounds without the tongue gestures sounds like /w/.
  3. F3 lives in the front space. MRI-based modelling found F3 is a resonance of the space in front of the palatal narrowing, enlarged by the space under the tongue (Espy-Wilson et al. 2000).
  4. Many tongue shapes, one result. Retroflex and bunched r give the same F1 to F3 (Delattre and Freeman 1968; Zhou et al. 2008); they differ in F4 and F5. The picture cannot tell which tongue shape the child used, and both are acceptable.

Typical values (summary)

  • Adults: r F3 about 1300 to 1950 Hz across studies; about 1700 to 1830 Hz in Espy-Wilson (1992); about 60 to 80% of the speaker’s own vowel F3 (Hagiwara 1995 as reported by Zhou et al. 2008).
  • Children 10 to 12, /ɝ/: F3 about 2077 Hz (boys) and 2259 Hz (girls), F2 about 1710 to 1740 Hz (Hillenbrand et al. 1995).
  • Correct consonant r in school-age children: F3 often about 2100 to 2700 Hz (working range derived from the studies; not a published norm).

Full tables: Typical values for r. The gap measure and z-scores: The F3-F2 gap. Word position: Position and context. Errors: What r errors look like.

How to tell it from

  • /w/: F3 stays high; F2 very low.
  • /l/: F3 high; abrupt edges.
  • /j/: F2 very high, F3 high; the gap is narrow because F2 is high.
  • Plain vowel /ʌ/ or /ɑ/ in a non-rhotic “bird” or “car”: F3 stays at vowel height.

On the Speak Up screen

  1. Find the r. Onset r: the start of voicing. “car”: the last third of the vowel. “bird”: the vowel middle. Use Scrub to hear where it is.
  2. Put a cursor at the lowest point of F3. That is where the research measures (Campbell et al. 2018; Harel et al. 2017; McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012).
  3. Read F3 first, then the gap. For a school-age child, F3 around 2000 to 2500 Hz with a gap of a few hundred Hz looks like a convincing r; F3 around 3000 Hz or more with a gap over about 1000 Hz looks like a glide or a plain vowel. These are working ranges, not cutoffs.
  4. Beware front vowels. /i ɪ j/ have narrow gaps too; confirm F3 itself dips.
  5. Compare with the child’s own vowels. A correct r F3 is roughly two-thirds of the child’s ordinary vowel F3 (Compare the child with themselves).
  6. Trust the bands over the dots. If F3 visibly bends toward F2 and the dots disagree, it is a tracking error.
  7. Short onsets. Onset r, and especially cluster r (“truck”, “tree”), may give only a few frames. Listeners are more lenient with short r (McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012).
  8. F4 and F5 (retroflex against bunched) are probably not usable: in children they are likely near or above 6 kHz (an inference, UNVERIFIED).

The Target sound tool highlights F2, F3 and the gap in the r window; Hz ranges shows age-matched bands where a checked study exists.

sections.title: The F3-F2 gap, normalization and z-scores
sections.body_html:
Why F3-F2 and not F3 alone

F3 falls as children grow and differs by sex, so one F3 cutoff misfits. F3-F2 combines the main cue (low F3) with the second cue (fairly high F2, which separates r from /w/ and /l/), and partly cancels size. It does not cancel it fully: in the larger Lee et al. data, F3-F2 still showed age and sex effects, so Flipsen et al. (2001) recommended z-scores by age and sex.

z-scores

z = (child’s gap minus group mean) divided by group SD. Higher z means a wider gap, so less r-like. Children 9 to 15 with residual r errors had a mean baseline z of 6.92 (Cialdella et al. 2020).

The “z less than 6.0” marker is not a correct/incorrect cutoff. Shriberg et al. (2001) built it to separate already-derhotacized tokens from adolescents with a history of speech delay from those with only an r error (sensitivity 85%, specificity 79%). Do not use it to score a token.

sections.title: r by position and context
sections.body_html:
r is not one target. Clinicians separate:

  • Onset (prevocalic): “red”, “rabbit”, “rocket”, “rain”, “ring”.
  • Between vowels: “carrot”, “very”.
  • After a vowel (postvocalic): “car”, “door”, “bear”.
  • Syllabic or vocalic: /ɝ/ “bird”, /ɚ/ “butter”.
  • Cluster: “truck”, “tree”, “green”.

What changes:

  • Depth. In adults, consonant r usually lowers F3 more than vocalic r (McGowan et al. 2004, as cited by McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012): McGowan’s adult had F3 1255 to 1655 Hz in “right” and “rag” against 1710 to 1931 Hz in “there” and “large”.
  • Lips. Onset r is usually rounded; postvocalic r often is not (McGowan et al. 2004; Espy-Wilson 1992).
  • Order of learning. Young children often get postvocalic and syllabic r before onset r (McGowan et al. 2004).
  • Duration. Vocalic r is longer than single onset r, which is longer than cluster r, and listeners are more lenient with the shorter forms (McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012). A millisecond norm for children’s onset r was not found (UNVERIFIED).
  • The next vowel sets where the F3 dip starts and ends: high F2 before /i ɪ/, low F2 before /u o/. The duration of the F3 movement stays similar across neighbouring consonants (Boyce and Espy-Wilson 1997).
  • Context still matters after normalising (Flipsen et al. 2001; Campbell et al. 2018). Compare like with like.

On the Speak Up screen: the window position follows the word (start, middle or end). For “truck” the r sits right after the /t/ burst and aspiration, so the F3 dip may begin inside the aspiration where there are no dots.

  1. Gliding, r to [w] (“wed”): F3 does not drop; F2 low; gap very wide. See Gliding.
  2. Derhotacized r (the residual error): F3 lowered a little but not enough, often about 2700 to 3200 Hz in a school-age child against 2100 to 2600 for correct tokens (McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012). Intermediate gap. See Derhotacization.
  3. Vocalic r errors (“bird” as [bʌd], “car” as [kɑ]): F3 stays at vowel height; no F3 fall at the end. See Vocalic r errors.
  4. r to [l]: F3 high, abrupt edges, l-like dips in the spectrum.
  5. Partly correct: F3 dips briefly, late or shallow, for example only at the end of a cluster.

sections.title: /w/ as in "wed", "one"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

A short, vowel-like start with low F1 and very low F2 (lower than /u/), then F2 rising into the vowel. F3 stays high and is often weak; the F3-F2 gap is very wide.

Why these frequencies

Lips closely rounded plus the tongue back raised. The lips lower every formant and the back tongue enlarges the front space, so F2 drops a long way. With no palatal or throat narrowing, F3 stays vowel-high. /w/ has lower F1 and F2 than /u/ (Espy-Wilson 1992).

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Adults, onset 381 848 2320 Espy-Wilson 1992
Adults, between vowels 349 771 2340 Espy-Wilson 1992
Children 3 to 4, onset about 3500 Dalston 1975 via McGowan et al. 2004

Child /w/ F2 was not found in a checked source (UNVERIFIED); expect it below the child’s /u/ F2, roughly 900 to 1300 Hz by scaling (an estimate). Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

What errors look like

/w/ itself is rarely in error by school age. It matters as the substitute for r and l (Gliding).

How to tell it from

/r/: is F3 low (r) or high (w)? F2 is low in both but much lower in /w/. Dalston (1975) found 3 to 4 year olds’ r and w overlapped in F1 and F2, while F3 still separated them. /l/: abrupt edges, F2 a little higher.

On the Speak Up screen

In gliding, the gap readout will be large, often over 1000 Hz. In 3 to 4 year olds automatic F3-F2 agrees only moderately with listeners (Ancel et al. 2023), so pair the number with your ear.

sections.title: /l/ as in "leaf", "ball"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

  • Light /l/ (word start, “leaf”): low F1, moderate F2, high F3. The formants often jump at the release instead of gliding, and the F3 to F4 region can look weak or patchy.
  • Dark /l/ (word end, “ball”): F2 low, close to F1 (an /o/ or /u/ colour), F3 high.

Why these frequencies

The tongue tip touches the ridge behind the teeth while air flows round one or both sides. The side channels act as branches that make antiresonances (energy dips), mostly in the F3 to F5 range (Stevens 1998), which push F3 up and weaken it. Dark /l/ adds a pulled-back tongue body, lowering F2; final /l/ shows more retraction than initial /l/ (Recasens 2012, as cited in later work). The tip contact releases fast, so the edges are abrupt; Espy-Wilson (1992) found many onset and between-vowel /l/s start or end with a sudden shift, though not all.

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Adults, onset 399 1074 2553 Espy-Wilson 1992
Adults, between vowels 445 1060 2640 Espy-Wilson 1992
Adults, after a vowel (dark) 465 898 2630 Espy-Wilson 1992
Children 3 to 4, onset about 3500 Dalston 1975 via McGowan et al. 2004

Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11 at a 90% criterion (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

What errors look like

  • Gliding /l/ to [w] or [j] (“wed” or “yed” for “led”): smooth glide instead of an abrupt edge; F2 low ([w]) or high ([j]).
  • Vocalized /l/ (“ball” as [bɔʊ]): no tip contact; F2 low, F3 high, smooth. Common in several dialects; check before scoring.

How to tell it from

/r/: F1 and F2 similar, F3 high for /l/, low for /r/. /w/: smooth rather than abrupt, F2 lower. /j/: F2 much higher.

On the Speak Up screen

Look for a sharp edge at the release and a thin or missing F3 band. The tracker may report a false F3 because LPC cannot model antiresonances. In the spectrum at the cursor, a valley in the 2 to 4 kHz range during the /l/ fits an antiresonance.

sections.title: /j/ as in "yes", "you"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

A brief start with very low F1 and very high F2, at or above /i/, then F2 falling into the next vowel.

Why these frequencies

The tongue body is raised and fronted toward the hard palate, a tighter /i/: front space short, back space large. /j/ has lower F1 than /i/ and usually higher F2 or F3, with fairly strong upper formants (Espy-Wilson 1992).

Typical values (Hz)

Group F1 F2 F3 Source
Adults, onset 317 2142 2827 Espy-Wilson 1992
Adults, between vowels 361 2270 2920 Espy-Wilson 1992
Reference: /i/ boys / girls 10 to 12 444 / 464 3028 / 3159 3602 / 3806 Hillenbrand et al. 1995

Child /j/ values were not found (UNVERIFIED); expect F2 near or above the child’s /i/, around 3000 Hz. Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

What errors look like

More often a substitute than a target: /l/ or /r/ to [j] in young children shows F2 shooting up to /i/ values.

How to tell it from

/r/: /j/ has a small gap with F3 high; r has a small gap with F3 low. If the gap is narrow and F3 is up near the child’s /i/ F3 (about 3500 Hz or more), it is /j/ or /i/, not r.

On the Speak Up screen

The narrowest-gap search can land on a /j/ or /i/. Check F3 height.
