sections.title: Stops: /p b t d k g/
sections.body_html:
What stops look like

A stop has up to four parts in time:

  1. Closure: the mouth is sealed. Blank for /p t k/. For /b d g/ there may be a voice bar (a thin dark band below about 300 to 500 Hz with pitch marks); English word-initial /b d g/ often lack it.
  2. Burst: a thin vertical spike of noise when the seal opens, a few ms to about 20 ms.
  3. Aspiration (/p t k/ at the start of a stressed syllable): weaker noise after the burst, no voicing, with faint bands of the next vowel.
  4. Transitions into the vowel: F1 rises out of the closure; F2 and F3 move from a place-specific start (Place of articulation).

Place: lips, tongue tip, tongue back

Place Stops Burst (first 10 to 20 ms) F2 at vowel onset
Lips /p b/ Weak, flat or falling: strongest low Below the vowel’s F2; rises into most vowels
Tongue tip /t d/ Rising: strongest high (often above 3 to 4 kHz in adults, higher in children) Near 1700 to 1800 Hz (adult); falls into back vowels
Tongue back /k g/ Compact: one strong mid peak (about 1.5 to 4 kHz in adults, higher before front vowels) F2 and F3 start close together (velar pinch)

Burst shapes from Stevens and Blumstein (1978) and Blumstein and Stevens (1979); loci from Delattre et al. (1955).

Voicing: VOT

Category VOT Adult means (Lisker and Abramson 1964, via Kim 2021)
/p t k/ stressed start Long lag, about 40 to 100+ ms /p/ 58, /t/ 70, /k/ 80 ms
/b d g/ start Short lag, about 0 to 25 ms, or prevoiced /b/ 1, /d/ 5, /g/ 21 ms
/p t k/ after /s/ Short lag Like /b d g/

Rule of thumb: in a 4 to 12 year old, a stressed initial /p t k/ with VOT under about 25 to 30 ms will usually be heard as /b d g/ (an adult-based boundary; UNVERIFIED as a child cutoff). More: Voicing.

Acquisition

Plosives as a class about 3;11 at a 90% criterion; /b p d/ by 2;0 to 2;11, /k g t/ by 3;0 to 3;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

On the Speak Up screen

Closure, burst and aspiration are crisp with the 6 ms window. Measure VOT from the burst to the first regular pulse on the waveform with two cursors (Cursor), not from the pitch line. No dots during voiceless closure or aspiration; read F2 onset from the first voiced frames. A voice bar may get an “F1” dot near 200 to 300 Hz that is not a vowel formant. Put the cursor on the burst and use the spectrum to judge rising (tip), one mid peak (back) or falling (lips).

sections.title: /p/ as in "pig", "cup"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Silent closure, a weak, flat or falling burst, then (at the start of a stressed syllable) aspiration noise, then F2 rising into the vowel. Word-final /p/ is often unreleased (no burst), which is normal.

Why these frequencies

Closure at the lips leaves no front space to shape the burst, so it is weak and low. Opening the lips raises all formants, so F2 rises into most vowels.

Typical values

VOT stressed initial, adults: mean 58 ms, range 20 to 120 ms (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). F2 locus about 720 Hz (adult, Delattre et al. 1955). Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

What errors look like

Short VOT with no aspiration (heard as /b/, prevocalic voicing); deletion at the end of a word (final consonant deletion).

How to tell it from

/b/: short VOT. /t/: rising burst, F2 starting near 1800 Hz. /f/: noise instead of silence and burst.

On the Speak Up screen

A weak burst is easy to miss in noise; zoom in and look for the closure gap.

sections.title: /b/ as in "big", "rabbit"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Closure (with or without a voice bar), a weak burst, a short VOT, F2 rising into the vowel.

Why these frequencies

As for /p/, with the vocal folds ready to vibrate at or soon after the release.

Typical values

VOT adults: mean about 1 ms for short-lag tokens; prevoiced tokens about -101 ms (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11.

What errors look like

Long VOT (heard as /p/); final devoicing (“cub” as “cup”: shorter vowel before it, no voicing in closure).

How to tell it from

/p/: VOT. /m/: murmur instead of silence, no burst. /d/, /g/: burst and F2 start.

On the Speak Up screen

In “rabbit” the /b/ is between vowels: often a short voiced closure with a voice bar throughout.

sections.title: /t/ as in "top", "rabbit"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Silent closure, a burst rising toward high frequencies, aspiration at the start of stressed syllables, F2 starting near the alveolar locus.

Why these frequencies

The tongue tip closes behind the teeth, leaving a small front space: the burst is strongest high.

Typical values

VOT stressed initial, adults: mean 70 ms, range 30 to 105 ms (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). F2 locus about 1800 Hz (adult; higher in children). Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11.

Normal variants: between vowels before an unstressed vowel (“butter”) /t/ becomes a flap; before /n/ or at the end of a word (“button”, “cat”) it often becomes a glottal stop or is unreleased (Zue and Laferriere 1979 studied these rules). These are not errors.

What errors look like

Backing to [k] (compact burst, F2 and F3 pinched); stopping produces /t/ for /s/; short VOT (heard as /d/).

How to tell it from

/k/: one mid peak in the burst, velar pinch. /d/: short VOT. /tʃ/: long /ʃ/-like noise after the burst. /s/: long noise and no closure.

On the Speak Up screen

Children’s /t/ burst carries much energy above 6 kHz; use Show all and the spectrum at the burst. In “rabbit” and “carrot” final /t/ may be unreleased or glottal.

sections.title: /d/ as in "door", "dog"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Closure (voice bar optional), a rising burst, short VOT, F2 starting near the alveolar locus.

Typical values

VOT adults: about 5 ms for short-lag tokens, about -102 ms prevoiced (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11.

What errors look like

Backing to [g]; velar assimilation (“guck” for “duck”); devoicing.

How to tell it from

/t/: VOT. /g/: compact burst. /n/: murmur instead of silence.

On the Speak Up screen

In “door” the F2 starts high and falls into the back vowel; then look for the F3 fall of the final r.

sections.title: /k/ as in "cat", "rocket"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Silent closure, a compact burst with one strong mid peak, often more than one burst spike, long aspiration, and F2 and F3 starting close together (the velar pinch).

Why these frequencies

The tongue back closes against the soft palate, leaving a larger front space whose resonance lines up with F2 or F3 of the next vowel. It is higher before front vowels, lower before back vowels.

Typical values

VOT stressed initial, adults: mean 80 ms, range 50 to 135 ms, the longest of the three (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11.

What errors look like

Fronting to [t]: a rising diffuse burst, no velar pinch, F2 near the alveolar locus.

How to tell it from

/t/: compare the child’s own /t/ and /k/ bursts with the spectrum at the cursor, and compare F2 at vowel onset.

On the Speak Up screen

Multiple burst spikes are normal for /k g/. In “rocket” and “truck” /k/ is a good place to check for fronting.

sections.title: /g/ as in "go", "big"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Closure (voice bar optional), compact burst, short VOT, velar pinch.

Typical values

VOT adults: about 21 ms short-lag, about -88 ms prevoiced (Lisker and Abramson 1964 via Kim 2021). Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11.

What errors look like

Fronting to [d]; devoicing to [k].

How to tell it from

/k/: VOT. /d/: rising burst. /ŋ/: murmur.

On the Speak Up screen

As for /k/.

sections.title: The flap [ɾ] as in "butter", "water"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

A very brief dip in energy between two vowels, usually voiced throughout, often with no visible burst; F1 drops and recovers.

Why

American English /t/ and /d/ between vowels before an unstressed vowel become a quick tap of the tongue tip (Zue and Laferriere 1979 describe the rule and its probabilities). The closure is roughly 10 to 40 ms (UNVERIFIED range).

What it is not

  • Not an error: a child saying a full [tʰ] in “water” is using a careful style.
  • In Spanish, the tap /ɾ/ is an r sound (ASHA Spanish phonemic inventory). A tapped r in an English word from a Spanish-English bilingual child is normal cross-language influence (Dialect and second language).

On the Speak Up screen

Look for a short dip in the intensity line and a break in the bands. The tracker may keep tracking straight through.

sections.title: The glottal stop [ʔ]
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Voicing stops abruptly, a short silence (or none), then restarts abruptly, often with one or a few irregular, widely spaced pulses (creak) either side. No oral burst and no place-specific transitions.

Why

The vocal folds close tightly and release. Nothing in the mouth is shaped, so there is no place cue.

Normal uses

Before a word-initial vowel in careful speech, “uh-oh”, and for /t/ before /n/ or at the end of a word (“button”, “cat”) in many American speakers (Ladefoged and Johnson 2015; Zue and Laferriere 1979). Not errors.

As an error

Glottal stops replacing oral stops (and sometimes fricatives) are a compensatory pattern in cleft palate speech: the child makes the sound below the leaky velopharyngeal port (ASHA, Cleft Lip and Palate). See Glottal replacement.

On the Speak Up screen

The pitch line drops out or jumps (creak causes octave errors); intensity dips abruptly; no burst on the waveform; dots absent or erratic.

sections.title: Fricatives: /f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h/
sections.body_html:
What fricatives look like

A stretch of random noise: speckle with no vertical stripes and no pitch, lasting roughly 80 to 200 ms in single words (UNVERIFIED range; longer at the end of a word).

  • Sibilants /s z ʃ ʒ/: loud, with noise concentrated in a band.
  • Non-sibilants /f v θ ð/: weak, noise spread thinly and flat.
  • Voiced /v ð z ʒ/ add a voice bar, stripes through the noise and pitch marks. In English they are often partly devoiced, especially at the end of a word; then the longer vowel before them and the shorter, weaker noise are the main cues (Stevens et al. 1992).

Why these frequencies

The noise is shaped by the space in front of the narrowing: smaller space, higher noise (Noise sources). /s/ is highest, /ʃ/ lower (further back, rounded lips), /f θ/ flat.

Measuring the noise

Spectral moments treat the noise spectrum as a distribution (Forrest et al. 1988): M1 centre of gravity, M2 spread, M3 skew, M4 peakedness. /s/: highest M1, focused, negative skew. /ʃ/: lower M1, focused, positive skew. /f θ/: spread out. Moments depend on the analysis range, so values from 16 kHz audio do not match values from 44.1 kHz. Shadle (2023) argues moments mix up peak location and noise floor and suggests peak and band-energy measures instead: a mid-frequency peak in 3 to 7 kHz plus low (0.55 to 3 kHz), mid (3 to 7 kHz) and high (7 to 11 kHz) band energies (Koenig et al. 2013). For young children Wong and Munson (2025) recommend a 3 to 9 kHz peak range.

Children

  • Normal-hearing children about 5;2: /s/ M1 7699 Hz, /ʃ/ 5223 Hz (Todd et al. 2011, analysed to 11 kHz).
  • 63 children 2;6 to 3;6: [s] M1 6976 Hz, peak (3 to 9 kHz) 6769 Hz; [ʃ] M1 4913 Hz, peak 4558 Hz (Wong and Munson 2025).
  • Children’s /s/-/ʃ/ difference is smaller than adults’ and changes sharply around 5 (Nissen and Fox 2005; Nittrouer 1995).
  • Toddlers transcribed as merging /s/ and /ʃ/ often still make a measurable difference: covert contrast (Li et al. 2009).

Acquisition (Crowe and McLeod 2020, 90% criterion)

/f/ 3;0 to 3;11; /v s z ʃ/ 4;0 to 4;11; /ð ʒ/ 5;0 to 5;11; /θ/ 6;0 to 6;11. Fricatives as a class about 6;11.

On the Speak Up screen

Sound Key energy in children Compact picture (0 to 6 kHz) Full view (to 11 kHz)
/ʃ ʒ/ Peak about 2.6 to 5.5 kHz Visible Visible
/s z/ Peak often 6.5 to 9.5 kHz Only the lower edge; peak off the top Peak usually visible
/f θ/ Flat, weak, to 8 kHz and beyond Faint grey, easy to miss Faint grey

No dots or pitch should appear during /s ʃ f θ/. Dots during /z/ follow the voice bar, not vowel formants. Spectral numbers from the 16 kHz copy are biased low and are not comparable with published child norms.

sections.title: /s/ as in "sun", "bus"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Loud, dense noise starting a few kHz up and getting darker toward the top; in children the darkest part is often at 7 to 9.5 kHz. No stripes, no pitch.

Why these frequencies

Tongue tip or blade at the ridge behind the teeth, a groove down the middle of the tongue, a tiny front space, and the air jet hitting the teeth: intense high noise.

Typical values

  • Adults: peak about 6 to 8 kHz (Jongman et al. 2000, range confirmed via a citing paper; exact mean UNVERIFIED).
  • Adolescents: mid-frequency peak about 5742 to 6320 Hz, about 4401 to 4843 Hz next to rounded sounds (Koenig et al. 2013 as quoted by Wong and Munson 2025).
  • Children about 5: M1 7699 Hz; one 6-year-old’s /s/ peaked at 9410 Hz in /se/ and 5727 Hz in /sɪ/ (Todd et al. 2011).
  • Children 2;6 to 3;6: M1 6976 Hz (Wong and Munson 2025).
  • Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

What errors look like

  • Interdental lisp: fainter, flatter, lower, like /θ/ (Lisps).
  • Lateral lisp: lower, more diffuse, “slushy” (Lateral lisp).
  • Palatal /s/: peak dropped toward /ʃ/ (Palatal /s/).
  • Stopping: gap and burst instead of noise (Stopping).
  • Deleted in clusters (“top” for “stop”) (Cluster reduction).

How to tell it from

/ʃ/: lower peak, compare with the child’s own /ʃ/; if the /s/ peak is at or below the /ʃ/ peak, the contrast is lost. /θ/: much weaker and flat. /t/: silence and a burst. /z/: voicing.

On the Speak Up screen

Use Show all (to 11 kHz); the compact picture cannot confirm a correct /s/, only flag one whose energy has moved down into view. A child’s /s/ peak clearly inside 0 to 6 kHz is suspicious (lowered: palatal, lateral, or a rounded context). The 16 kHz copy that Arti and the measures use loses everything above 8 kHz, and listeners need about 9 kHz of bandwidth to perceive child /s/ well (Stelmachowicz et al. 2001). Always use your ear.

sections.title: /z/ as in "zoo", "is"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

/s/-like noise plus a voice bar, stripes and pitch. Often partly devoiced at the end of a word (“is”, “dogs”), where it may look like /s/ with a longer vowel before it.

Typical values

Noise peak like /s/ (Jongman et al. 2000). Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11.

What errors look like

Stopping to [d] (expected gone by about 4, ASHA); devoicing in the middle of words; lisps as for /s/.

How to tell it from

/s/: at the end of a word, voicing is often weak in both; the longer preceding vowel marks /z/ (Raphael 1972). /ð/: much weaker noise.

On the Speak Up screen

Dots during /z/ follow the voice bar; ignore them.

sections.title: /ʃ/ as in "shoe", "fish"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Loud noise with a clear lower edge and a darkest region lower than /s/: about 2.5 to 4.5 kHz in adults, often above 4 kHz in children.

Why these frequencies

The narrowing is further back (behind the alveolar ridge) and the lips round: a bigger front space and a lower peak. Jongman et al. (2000) describe a mid-frequency peak near 2.5 to 3 kHz in adults, often linked to the next vowel’s F3.

Typical values

Children about 5: M1 5223 Hz; one 6-year-old’s peaks 3919 Hz (/ʃi/) and 2627 Hz (/ʃu/) (Todd et al. 2011). Children 2;6 to 3;6: M1 4913 Hz, peak about 4486 to 4558 Hz (Wong and Munson 2025). Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11.

What errors look like

Fronting to [s] (peak higher than the child’s /ʃ/ should be); stopping to [t]; lisp-like distortions.

How to tell it from

/s/: higher peak. /tʃ/: a gap and burst before shorter noise.

On the Speak Up screen

Fully visible in the compact picture. A good place to compare with the child’s /s/.

sections.title: /ʒ/ as in "measure", "beige"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

/ʃ/-like noise plus voicing.

Typical values

Acquired by 5;0 to 5;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020). Rare in English words, so children have less practice with it.

What errors look like

Replaced by [dʒ], [z] or [ʃ].

How to tell it from

/dʒ/: gap and burst first. /ʃ/: no voicing.

sections.title: /f/ as in "fun", "leaf"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Weak, flat, faint grey noise spread over a wide range, no clear peak.

Why these frequencies

The narrowing is between the lower lip and upper teeth, leaving almost no front space to shape the noise (Jongman et al. 2000).

Typical values

Weak, high spread (M2); spectral peak values unreliable (adult mean about 7.7 kHz recalled, UNVERIFIED). Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11.

What errors look like

Stopping to [p] (expected gone by about 3, ASHA).

How to tell it from

/θ/: acoustically very similar; listeners rely partly on the transitions into the vowel and on what they see. /s/: much louder, higher. /p/: gap and burst.

On the Speak Up screen

Easy to miss; zoom in and raise your attention to faint grey. The spectrogram alone cannot reliably separate /f/ from /θ/.

sections.title: /v/ as in "van", "very"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Weak noise with voicing; often so weak it looks almost like a vowel-like voiced stretch with a dip in intensity.

Typical values

Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11.

What errors look like

Stopping to [b] (expected gone by about 4, ASHA); devoicing to [f].

How to tell it from

/b/: closure and burst. /w/: smooth formant glide, no noise.

On the Speak Up screen

In “very” the /v/ is short and followed by a vowel then r.

sections.title: /θ/ as in "thumb", "bath"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Weak, flat noise like /f/.

Why these frequencies

Tongue tip at or between the teeth: almost no front space.

Typical values

Acquired by 6;0 to 6;11, the latest English consonant (mean 77 months at a 90% criterion, Crowe and McLeod 2020). Adult spectral peak about 7 to 7.5 kHz recalled (UNVERIFIED).

What errors look like

Replaced by [f] (“fumb”) or [t] (stopping). [f] for /θ/ is also reported as a dialect feature in some varieties of English (UNVERIFIED for specific dialects here); check the child’s dialect before scoring (Dialect and second language).

How to tell it from

/f/: very similar acoustically. /s/: much louder and higher; an interdental lisp makes /s/ sound /θ/-like.

On the Speak Up screen

Use as the comparison for a suspected interdental lisp.

sections.title: /ð/ as in "this", "brother"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Very weak voiced noise; often almost no noise at all, more like a weak voiced stretch, especially in fast speech.

Typical values

Acquired by 5;0 to 5;11.

What errors look like

Stopping to [d] (“dis”), common in young children and also reported as a dialect feature in some varieties (UNVERIFIED for specific dialects here; see Dialect and second language).

How to tell it from

/d/: closure and burst. /v/: very similar.

sections.title: /h/ as in "hat", "ahead"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Faint noise showing the next vowel’s formant bands (a whispered version of the vowel). Between vowels (“ahead”) it is often voiced and breathy.

Why

The noise is made at the vocal folds and shaped by the whole tract, which is already in the vowel’s shape.

Typical values

Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11. Koenig (2000) found fully voiced /h/ most common in men and /h/ voicing most variable in 5-year-olds.

What errors look like

Deletion (“at” for “hat”: the vowel starts abruptly). /h/ replacing other fricatives can be a compensatory pattern in cleft palate speech (ASHA lists glottal fricatives among errors made behind the velopharyngeal port).

On the Speak Up screen

Faint, no pitch, no dots; easy to miss at low recording levels.

sections.title: Affricates: /tʃ dʒ/
sections.body_html:
An affricate is a stop and a fricative in one: closure, burst, then /ʃ/-like noise, all in one segment. The noise is shorter than a standalone /ʃ/ and rises fast.

Rise time (from noise onset to its loudest point) is shorter for affricates than fricatives, but Howell and Rosen (1983) found it varies with the material and that “no single value of rise time” separates them; use it only as a relative cue within the same child and task.

Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11 at a 90% criterion (Crowe and McLeod 2020).

On the Speak Up screen: gap and burst are clear; the noise is inside 0 to 6 kHz. On the waveform or intensity line, an abrupt jump in loudness after the gap suggests an affricate; a ramp suggests a fricative.

sections.title: /tʃ/ as in "chip", "watch"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Silent closure, burst, then about /ʃ/-like noise (adult peak about 2.5 to 4.5 kHz, higher in children), shorter than a lone /ʃ/.

Typical values

Noise shorter than /ʃ/ (direction standard; values UNVERIFIED). Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11.

What errors look like

  • Deaffrication to [ʃ] (“ship” for “chip”): no gap or burst; noise rises gradually. Usually gone by about 4 (ASHA).
  • Stopping to [t]: gap and burst but no noise after it. Expected gone by about 5 (ASHA).
  • Fronting to [ts]: noise higher than the child’s own /ʃ/.

How to tell it from

/ʃ/: no closure. /t/: no long noise.

sections.title: /dʒ/ as in "jump", "bridge"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Closure (voice bar optional), burst, voiced /ʒ/-like noise.

Typical values

Acquired by 4;0 to 4;11.

What errors look like

Devoicing to [tʃ] (no voice bar, longer noise); deaffrication to [ʒ]; stopping to [d].

How to tell it from

/tʃ/: voicing and shorter noise. /ʒ/: no closure.

sections.title: Nasals: /m n ŋ/
sections.body_html:
What nasals look like

  • Murmur: voiced (stripes, pitch) with a strong low nasal formant (adults roughly 250 to 300 Hz) and much weaker energy above: a dark low bar under a pale upper region.
  • Abrupt edges where the mouth opens or closes: a sharp change in the spectrogram and a drop in intensity.
  • Transitions in the next vowel like the stops: /m/ like /b/, /n/ like /d/, /ŋ/ like /g/.
  • Vowels before a nasal are partly nasalized; that is normal.

Why these frequencies

The throat plus nose make one long, soft, absorbent tube: a low first resonance and damped energy above. The closed mouth is a side branch that cancels energy at its own resonance (an antiformant). Fujimura (1962) showed the antiformant’s location is what distinguishes the three nasals: lowest for /m/ (longest closed mouth), higher for /n/, highest for /ŋ/ (Nasal coupling). Kurowski and Blumstein (1987) found place could be read from how energy changes from the murmur to the release: more change in a low band (Bark 5 to 7) for /m/ and a higher band (Bark 11 to 14) for /n/, classifying over 89% of tokens.

Typical values (adults; children higher in proportion to tract size)

Nasal Murmur first formant Antiformant Status
/m/ about 250 to 300 Hz about 750 to 1250 Hz Textbook range (Kent and Read 2002), UNVERIFIED; a modelling study estimated about 1100 Hz (Mehta et al. 2012)
/n/ about 250 to 300 Hz about 1450 to 2200 Hz Textbook range, UNVERIFIED
/ŋ/ about 250 to 300 Hz above about 3000 Hz UNVERIFIED

Acquisition: nasals as a class about 3;11 (Crowe and McLeod 2020); /m n/ 2;0 to 2;11; /ŋ/ 3;0 to 3;11.

On the Speak Up screen

The murmur is easy to see. Dots during the murmur are nasal resonances, not vowel formants: an “F1” dot near 250 to 300 Hz is the nasal formant. The antiformant may show as a pale notch in the spectrum at the cursor, but the 6 ms window and high child pitch smear it; use the vowel transitions for place instead.

sections.title: /m/ as in "man", "jump"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low murmur with abrupt edges; F2 rises into most vowels after it (lip place).

Typical values

Antiformant lowest of the nasals (Nasals). Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11.

What errors look like

Denasalized to [b] (Hyponasality).

How to tell it from

/n/: F2 transitions (alveolar locus) and the murmur-to-release change. /b/: closure and burst instead of a murmur.

sections.title: /n/ as in "no", "rain"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low murmur with abrupt edges; F2 transitions toward the alveolar locus.

Typical values

Acquired by 2;0 to 2;11.

What errors look like

Denasalized to [d]; nasal assimilation spreading /n/ to other consonants.

How to tell it from

/m/, /ŋ/: transitions. /d/: burst.

On the Speak Up screen

In “rain” the vowel before /n/ is nasalized; its F1 may look weak or doubled.

sections.title: /ŋ/ as in "ring", "sing"
sections.body_html:
What it should look like

Low murmur at the end of the vowel, with the velar pinch (F2 and F3 coming together) at the vowel end.

Typical values

Acquired by 3;0 to 3;11. Only at the end of syllables in English.

What errors look like

Replaced by [n] (“runnin’”), which is a normal informal or dialect form in many varieties, not necessarily an error; or by [ŋg].

How to tell it from

/n/: no velar pinch. /g/: burst.

On the Speak Up screen

In “ring” look at the end of the /ɪ/ for F2 and F3 converging.

sections.title: Error patterns
sections.body_html: Each pattern below gives: what the child does, what it looks like on the picture, how to tell it from look-alikes, the usual causes, and the usual age by which it is gone. Elimination ages come from the ASHA Practice Portal table of phonological patterns (which cites Bowen 2011, Peña-Brooks and Hegde 2015, Shipley and McAfee 2016); ASHA notes that these ages “can vary greatly in each child”.

sections.title: All patterns at a glance
sections.body_html:

Gliding “wabbit” 6 to 7 F3 stays high in r; F2 low
Derhotacization r sounds “off” Not a developmental pattern past about 8 F3 lowered only part way
Vocalic r errors “bud” for “bird” With r generally No F3 fall in the vowel
Stopping “tee” for “see” /f s/ 3; /z v/ 4; /ʃ tʃ dʒ ð/ 5 Gap and burst instead of noise
Fronting “tat” for “cat” 4 Rising burst, no velar pinch
Backing “kop” for “top” Not typical at any age Compact burst on a tip target
Deaffrication “ship” for “chip” 4 No gap or burst before the noise
Cluster reduction “top” for “stop” With /s/: 5; without: 4 One consonant missing
Final consonant deletion “bu” for “bus” 3 Vowel ends with nothing after it
Weak syllable deletion “nana” for “banana” 4 One fewer vowel hump
Assimilation “guck” for “duck” 3 A consonant copies another in the word
Voicing errors “big” for “pig” Varies VOT in the wrong range
Lisps “thun” for “sun” Not a developmental pattern /s/ noise lower or flatter
Hypernasality, nasal emission Nasal-sounding vowels Not developmental Weak bursts and noise; dull vowels
Glottal replacement “ba-ʔ” for “bat” Not developmental No burst, creaky break

sections.title: Gliding
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Replaces a liquid (/r/ or /l/) with a glide ([w] or [j]): “wed” for “red”, “wabbit”, “yeg” for “leg”.

What it looks like

  • r to [w]: F3 stays high (at the child’s vowel F3, about 3000 to 3500 Hz) instead of dipping; F2 is low (rounded lips with a back tongue); the F3-F2 gap is very wide; smooth F2 rise into the vowel.
  • l to [w]: the abrupt /l/ edge becomes a smooth glide.
  • r or l to [j]: F2 shoots up toward /i/.

How to tell it from

  • Derhotacized r (Derhotacization): F3 drops part way. Many distorted r’s sound w-like, and listeners disagree where gliding ends and distortion begins. F3 height alone cannot separate them; compare with the child’s own /w/ in “one” or “wet”.
  • Labialized r: strong lip rounding with some tongue gesture; F3 may dip a little.

Usual causes

A developmental phonological pattern in young children. Persisting with other patterns suggests a phonological disorder.

Age

ASHA’s table: gone by about 6 to 7. Some tables (Bowen, citing Grunwell) give about 5. /ɹ/ acquired 5;0 to 5;11 at a 90% criterion (Crowe and McLeod 2020). Dalston (1975) found 3 to 4 year olds’ correct r already had F3 near 2500 Hz against about 3500 Hz for /w/.

On the Speak Up screen

Gap readout large, often over 1000 Hz. For 3 to 4 year olds, automatic F3-F2 is only a modest guide (Ancel et al. 2023).

sections.title: Derhotacization (distorted r)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Attempts r but the r-colour is weak: the sound is “r-ish but off”, not a clear [w]. Often called the residual r error; Shriberg’s classification calls it SE-/r/ (Shriberg et al. 2010).

What it looks like

F3 is lowered a little, not enough: a school-age child might show F3 about 2700 to 3200 Hz against 2100 to 2600 for correct tokens (McAllister Byun and Hitchcock 2012). The gap is in between. Because F3 can be partly lowered, these errors sit on a continuum, which is why gradient measures (z-scored gap, rating scales) suit them better than right or wrong.

Usual causes

Tongue tip or body not raised far enough, tongue root not pulled back, the space under the tongue missing, or the narrowing too far back. Context matters: many children manage r in some words (for example after a velar, or the vowel in “bird”) and not others. Probe several contexts.

Age and course

Errors persisting past about 8 to 9 are residual. Up to 75% may resolve on their own by the end of high school; 1 to 2% of young adults still have them (Flipsen 2015).

On the Speak Up screen

Compare the token with the child’s best r and with their non-r vowels (Compare the child with themselves). Children 9 to 15 with residual r errors had a mean z of 6.92 at baseline (Cialdella et al. 2020).

sections.title: Vocalic r errors
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Drops the r-colour in /ɝ/ (“bird” as [bʌd]), /ɚ/ (“butter” as [bʌtə]) and the r endings of “car”, “door”, “bear”.

What it looks like

F3 stays at vowel height throughout; in “car” there is no F3 fall at the end. Sometimes the ending becomes [ʊ] or [o]: F2 falls but F3 does not.

How to tell it from

Non-rhotic dialects drop postvocalic r normally (Dialect and second language). If onset r is good and only postvocalic r is missing, check dialect first.

On the Speak Up screen

Look at the last third of the vowel in “car”, “door”, “bear” for an F3 fall.

sections.title: Stopping
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Replaces a fricative or affricate with a stop: “tee” for “see”, “pun” for “fun”.

What it looks like

A silent (or voice-bar) gap and a burst where there should be continuous noise. A short aspiration after the burst can look like a brief fricative: check duration (aspiration is tens of ms; a real fricative is longer and, for sibilants, much louder).

How to tell it from

An affricate: gap, burst and long noise. A correct fricative with a soft start.

Usual causes and age

Developmental, most common at 3 to 5. ASHA: /f s/ by 3; /z v/ by 4; /ʃ tʃ dʒ ð/ by 5. Persisting suggests a phonological disorder. Also seen with hearing loss, because fricative noise is high and weak.

On the Speak Up screen

Very clear: a blank gap and a spike with no speckled noise.

sections.title: Fronting (velar to alveolar)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Says /k g/ as [t d]: “tat” for “cat”, “dough” for “go”.

What it looks like

On a /k g/ target: a diffuse, rising burst instead of one compact mid peak; F2 and F3 do not start together (no velar pinch); F2 starts near the alveolar locus.

Covert contrast

Some children transcribed as fronting still make measurably different /k/ and /t/ (UNVERIFIED for velars specifically in this research; shown for /s ʃ/ by Li et al. 2009). Gibbon (1999) found that 12 of 17 school-age children with speech sound disorders studied with electropalatography used undifferentiated tongue gestures (tip, body and sides contacting together) that transcription does not reliably detect. A child with a hidden contrast has something to build on.

Usual causes and age

Developmental, gone by about 4 (ASHA). Persisting suggests a phonological disorder.

On the Speak Up screen

Compare the child’s own /t/ and /k/ bursts in the spectrum at the cursor, and the F2 dots on the first voiced frames.

sections.title: Backing (alveolar to velar)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Says tip sounds further back: “kop” for “top”; /s/ backed toward [ʃ] or a velar-like noise.

What it looks like

A compact mid burst on /t d/ targets; F2 and F3 pinched at vowel onset; a lower noise peak for /s/.

Usual causes

Not a typical developmental pattern, so it is a flag for a phonological disorder. Can be compensatory in cleft palate speech (ASHA lists mid-dorsum palatal stops among compensatory errors). Hearing loss association UNVERIFIED here.

sections.title: Deaffrication
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Says an affricate as a fricative: “ship” for “chip”, “zhump” for “jump”.

What it looks like

No silent gap and no burst; the noise rises gradually like a fricative.

Age

Gone by about 4 (ASHA).

On the Speak Up screen

Check the waveform: an abrupt jump in loudness after a gap means affricate; a ramp means fricative.

sections.title: Cluster reduction
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Drops one consonant of a cluster: “top” for “stop”, “tuck” for “truck”, “tee” for “tree”.

What it looks like

One of the cluster’s consonants is missing in time. For /st/ to [t]: no /s/ noise before the gap. For /tɹ/ to [t]: no F3 dip after the /t/.

A clue worth checking: /t/ after /s/ is normally short lag (unaspirated). If “stop” said as [tɔp] still has a short-lag /t/, the child may be aiming for the cluster (UNVERIFIED as a documented developmental finding). In /tɹ/ clusters the r is short and may sit inside the aspiration (Klatt 1975 found aspiration in clusters with sonorants).

Development

Smit (1993): the youngest children reduce clusters; somewhat older children keep both but err on one; older children get them right. In obstruent plus approximant clusters (“tree”, “green”) reduction was mostly to the obstruent.

Age

With /s/: about 5; without /s/: about 4 (ASHA).

On the Speak Up screen

Easy to see, but a weak or very high /s/ may be partly off the compact picture: use Show all before calling it deleted.

sections.title: Final consonant deletion
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Leaves off the last consonant: “bu” for “bus”, “ca” for “cat”.

What it looks like

The vowel fades with no closure, burst, noise or murmur after it.

Hidden marking

Look at the vowel: F2 moving toward a locus at its end, or a longer vowel before a voiced target, can mean the child marks the consonant covertly. Weismer, Dinnsen and Elbert (1981) found two of three children who omitted final stops still made vowel length depend on the omitted stop’s voicing.

Caution

Unreleased final stops are normal in English (“cat” with no final burst). No burst is not deletion if a closure (silence after the vowel cuts off, with transitions) is present.

Age

Gone by about 3 (ASHA). Persisting is a clear flag for a phonological disorder.

sections.title: Weak syllable deletion
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Drops an unstressed syllable: “nana” for “banana”, “puter” for “computer”.

What it looks like

Count the vowel humps in the intensity line and the voiced stretches in the pitch line: one fewer than the target.

Age

Gone by about 4 (ASHA).

sections.title: Assimilation (consonant harmony)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

One consonant takes on features of another in the word: “guck” for “duck” (velar), “mummy” type nasal spread (“money” for “funny”).

What it looks like

A burst or murmur matching another consonant in the word instead of its own place or manner.

Age

Gone by about 3 (ASHA).

sections.title: Voicing and devoicing
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Voices a voiceless sound (“big” for “pig”) or devoices a voiced one (“bet” for “bed”, “pig” for “big”).

What it looks like

  • Prevocalic voicing: VOT on /p t k/ targets in the short-lag range (under about 25 to 30 ms), no aspiration noise.
  • Devoicing: long-lag VOT on /b d g/; at the end of a word, a shorter vowel before it and a voiceless closure with a strong burst.

Normal variation

English /b d g/ are often short lag (no voice bar), and final voiced sounds are often partly devoiced in adults. Judge by the contrast within the child’s own tokens, not by the voice bar alone. Vowel length is a strong cue for final voicing (Raphael 1972).

Usual causes

Developmental (the stages of Macken and Barton 1980), phonological disorder, motor timing problems (VOT variability is discussed in childhood apraxia; UNVERIFIED here), hearing loss. Young children’s voicing control is still variable (Koenig 2000).

On the Speak Up screen

Measure burst to first pulse on the waveform with two cursors; do not use the pitch line.

sections.title: Interdental (frontal) lisp
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Says /s z/ with the tongue tip between or against the front teeth, sounding /θ/-like.

What it looks like

The /s/ noise is fainter, flatter and lower, with no strong darkening near the top, and the intensity during the /s/ drops toward vowel level or below (direction from fricative acoustics, Jongman et al. 2000; specific lisp spectra UNVERIFIED in this research).

Usual causes

An articulation (motor) error. Often linked clinically to tongue thrust, open bite or missing front teeth around 6 to 8 (UNVERIFIED beyond ASHA’s mention of malocclusion as a screening item).

On the Speak Up screen

One of the few /s/ errors the compact picture can catch. Compare with the child’s /θ/ in “thumb”.

sections.title: Dentalized /s/
sections.body_html: The tongue tip touches the back of the upper teeth rather than going between them. The spectrum is somewhat flatter and the peak lower than a good /s/, but less so than an interdental lisp (UNVERIFIED). Often perceptually mild.

sections.title: Lateral lisp (lateralized /s/)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Lets air escape over the sides of the tongue, giving a slushy or “wet” sound. ASHA uses lateral /s/ as its example of a distortion.

What it looks like

Reported signs: a lower main peak, more diffuse noise, and sometimes low-frequency energy (UNVERIFIED: the acoustic literature on children’s lateral /s/ is small and was not located).

Usual causes

An articulation (motor) error, not a developmental phonological pattern.

On the Speak Up screen

Noise seems to start lower (down toward 2 to 3 kHz), may look closer to the child’s /ʃ/. Your perceptual judgment is primary.

sections.title: Palatal /s/
sections.body_html: The tongue body rises toward the palate and /s/ moves toward /ʃ/. The peak drops toward the /ʃ/ range, often inside the compact picture. This is also the usual pattern of /s/-/ʃ/ collapse. A visible peak below 5 to 6 kHz in a child’s /s/ is a good flag; compare with the child’s own /ʃ/. Some children who sound merged still make a small measurable difference (covert contrast, Li et al. 2009).

sections.title: Hypernasality and nasal emission
sections.body_html:
What the child does

  • Hypernasality: too much nasal resonance on vowels and voiced oral sounds.
  • Nasal emission: air escaping through the nose on pressure consonants (stops, fricatives, affricates); a “nasal rustle” when the gap is small (ASHA).

What it looks like

  • Hypernasal vowels: an extra low nasal peak (roughly 250 to 450 Hz, Chen 1997), weaker and wider F1, more energy between F1 and F2 and less in the F2 to F3 region (Kataoka et al. 1996). A1-P0 drops by about 6 to 8 dB for nasalized vowels (Chen 1997), but fails when F1 and the nasal peak coincide, as in low vowels and high child voices (Styler 2017).
  • Nasal emission: weak bursts, weak or short noise, extra noise during stops and fricatives.

Usual causes

Cleft palate (repaired or not), submucous cleft, velopharyngeal insufficiency after adenoidectomy, neurological causes, or learned. Phoneme-specific nasal emission affects only certain sounds, usually fricatives, and is learned, not structural (ASHA). Obligatory errors (from structure) need physical management; compensatory errors (learned) need therapy (ASHA).

Limits

A single microphone cannot separate oral from nasal sound. The clinical standards are perceptual rating, nasometry and nasopharyngoscopy (ASHA). Speak Up is not a nasality measure.

On the Speak Up screen

Dots on hypernasal vowels may show a false low “F1” near 250 to 450 Hz. Weak bursts and weak noise are visible.

sections.title: Hyponasality (denasalization)
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Not enough nasal resonance: “bad” for “man”, as with a cold.

What it looks like

A stop burst replaces the abrupt nasal edge; no low murmur bar.

Usual causes

Enlarged adenoids, a blocked nose; usually not a phonological error. Refer for medical review if persistent.

sections.title: Glottal replacement and other compensatory errors
sections.body_html:
What the child does

Replaces oral stops (and sometimes fricatives) with glottal stops, or uses pharyngeal fricatives, because enough mouth pressure could not be built (cleft palate, velopharyngeal insufficiency). ASHA: compensatory errors keep manner but change place, and can persist after surgical repair.

What it looks like

On stop targets: no oral burst and no place-matching F2 transitions; abrupt voicing stop and start with creaky, irregular pulses. Pharyngeal fricatives appear as low noise with high F1 in the next vowel (UNVERIFIED acoustic description).

Not to confuse with

Normal glottal /t/ in “button” or “cat” (Glottal stop).

On the Speak Up screen

Pitch line breaks or jumps, no burst spike, erratic dots near the event.

sections.title: Motor speech signs (apraxia, dysarthria)
sections.body_html:
Not diagnosable from one recording. ASHA describes childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) as a neurological disorder in which “the precision and consistency of movements during speech production are impaired”, and notes there are “currently no validated diagnostic features” separating it from other speech sound disorders. Consensus features include inconsistent errors on consonants and vowels across repeated productions, lengthened and disrupted transitions between sounds, and inappropriate prosody, especially stress. Dysarthria involves weakness, slowness or incoordination, often with voice, resonance or breathing differences. Shriberg’s classification gives motor speech disorders their own branch (Shriberg et al. 2010).

Patterns that justify a closer look, if seen across several words: very different formant tracks for the same word repeated; long or broken transitions; atypical vowel formants in non-target words; unusual pitch and intensity contours or stress. These are prompts for referral, not findings.

sections.title: Dialect and second language: differences are not disorders
sections.body_html:
ASHA’s position is that no dialect of English is a disorder (Social Dialects, 1983), and that a speech sound disorder is judged against the rules of the child’s own languages and dialects (Practice Portal). The 1983 statement also says ASHA does not encourage mass screening and enrollment of dialect speakers for intervention, which applies directly to a school screening tool.

Variety Feature Do not
Non-rhotic English (parts of New England, New York City, some Southern US, most of England, Australia) No r after a vowel (“car” as [kɑː]); onset r present Score postvocalic r “omission” as an error
African American English Postvocalic r may be vocalized or dropped; varies by speaker and community Score these as errors; a true distortion is still possible and is judged against AAE rules (Velleman and Pearson 2010)
Spanish-English bilinguals Spanish has a tap /ɾ/ and a trill /r/, no English approximant /ɹ/ (ASHA) Score a tap or trill in an English word as a disorder
Other languages Tap, trill, uvular and other r sounds Assume the English approximant is the only acceptable r for a child still learning English
British and other Englishes Labiodental [ʋ] for r in some speakers (prevalence UNVERIFIED) Assume every labialized r is an error

On the Speak Up screen: Arti was trained on New York and New Jersey American English, with rhotic listeners as judges. A non-rhotic “car” shows no F3 dip and Arti may call it incorrect: a model limit, not a finding. Note the child’s home language and dialect and score against it.

sections.title: Development, causes and treatment
sections.body_html: When sounds are usually mastered, when an error is expected for the child’s age, what causes errors, and how treatment relates to what the screen shows. Every age is a population benchmark, not a deadline for an individual child.

sections.title: Age of acquisition, every consonant
sections.body_html:
Crowe and McLeod (2020): review of 15 US studies, 18,907 children, 90% criterion.

Age band Consonants
2;0 to 2;11 /b n m p h w d/
3;0 to 3;11 /ɡ k f t ŋ j/
4;0 to 4;11 /v dʒ s tʃ l ʃ z/
5;0 to 5;11 /ɹ ð ʒ/
6;0 to 6;11 /θ/

Class means: plosives, nasals and glides about 3;11; affricates about 4;11; liquids about 5;11; fricatives about 6;11. From the paper’s Table 2: /ɹ/ mean 66.58 months (SD 18.62, range 30 to 96); /l/ 53.75 months (24 to 60); /θ/ 77.00 months (72 to 96).

Shriberg’s groups (Shriberg 1993, lists confirmed via Shriberg et al. 1997): Early 8 /m b j n w d p h/; Middle 8 /t ŋ k g f v tʃ dʒ/; Late 8 /ʃ θ s z ð l r ʒ/.

Why studies disagree. Different criteria (50, 75 or 90% of children), positions, tasks and regions. Smit et al. (1990), Iowa and Nebraska, found 90% of children correct on r only by about 8 (as summarised by McGowan et al. 2004 and Campbell et al. 2018).

sections.title: When phonological patterns usually stop
sections.body_html: The usual ages by which common patterns are gone are in All patterns at a glance (ASHA table). ASHA notes these ages “can vary greatly in each child”, and other sources shift them by six months to a year. A pattern that persists well past its usual age, or an atypical pattern such as backing, suggests a phonological disorder.

sections.title: Development of r
sections.body_html:
r is one of the last consonants mastered.

Source What it reports
Crowe and McLeod (2020) /ɹ/ acquired by 5;0 to 5;11 at a 90% criterion
Smit et al. (1990) 90% correct by about 8 (as summarised by McGowan et al. 2004); exact position-by-sex ages UNVERIFIED (paywalled)
ASHA table Gliding gone by 6 to 7

Position. Young children often get postvocalic and syllabic r before onset r (McGowan et al. 2004; Smit 1993 as cited there). In clusters (“tree”, “green”) the youngest reduce to the obstruent (Smit 1993).

A reading of the evidence for screening (a summary of the sources, not a published cutoff table):

Child’s age r gliding or distortion Usual reading
Under about 5 Gliding Usually expected; look at the whole sound system
About 5 to 6 r only Common; many still learning; monitor and rescreen
About 6 to 8 Persistent r errors A minority of typical children not yet at criterion; weigh other errors, intelligibility, perception, concern, impact
Over about 8 to 9 Any consistent r error Past the usual window: a residual error

Local eligibility rules always govern service decisions. Speak Up’s gliding flag follows the ASHA 6 to 7 figure.

sections.title: Residual errors and classification
sections.body_html:
• Residual speech sound errors (RSSE or RSSD): errors persisting past the age typical children master the sound; most research uses about 8 to 9.
  • Shriberg’s Speech Disorders Classification System (Shriberg et al. 2010): Speech Delay (3 to 9 year olds with deletions and substitutions that usually normalise with treatment); Speech Errors (distortions, usually sibilants or liquids, with subtypes SE-/s/ and SE-/r/); Motor Speech Disorder (apraxia, dysarthria, not otherwise specified); Persistent Speech Disorder for children over 9, with suffixes showing history.
  • Shriberg et al. (2001), as summarised by Campbell et al. (2018), found normalised F3-F2 separated r errors in children with a history of speech delay from isolated r errors.

sections.title: How common are speech sound errors
sections.body_html:
Population Estimate Source
Ages 4 to 6, any speech sound disorder 2.1% to 23% (depends on definition) ASHA Practice Portal
Age 6, speech delay 3.8% Shriberg, Tomblin and McSweeny 1999
Age 8, persistent speech sound disorder 3.6% (UK cohort) Wren et al. 2016
Young adults, residual errors 1% to 2% ASHA; Flipsen 2015
Sex ratio, grade school about 2 boys to 1 girl ASHA

A precise prevalence of r-only residual errors in US school children was not confirmed (UNVERIFIED).

sections.title: Hearing the difference: perception
sections.body_html:
Some, not all, children with r errors have trouble hearing correct from incorrect r, especially in their own speech.

  • Children with residual r errors judged misarticulated r poorly, their own and others’, and had broad r categories (Shuster 1998, as summarised by Preston et al. 2015).
  • In a school-age sample (9 to 14), children with residual r errors did not differ significantly from typical peers on a perception test, though more performed at chance (22% against 5%, not significant). Perception and production were not significantly correlated in another sample (Preston et al. 2015).

A child who says “that sounded right” when it did not fits this literature, not a lack of effort. It is one reason for visual feedback.

sections.title: Causes and associated factors
sections.body_html:
Most children with speech sound errors have no identifiable cause. ASHA notes it is “often difficult to clearly differentiate between articulation and phonological errors.”

Leans phonological Leans articulatory (motor)
Several patterns across sound classes (gliding of r and l, fronting, stopping) One or two sounds only (r, s)
Substitution of another phoneme Distortion: attempted sound that misses
Younger child Older child
Correct in some contexts
Cause Typical patterns
Structural Cleft palate, submucous cleft, VPI (nasal emission, hypernasality, glottal stops); malocclusion and missing teeth (lisps); ankyloglossia screened (ASHA)
Hearing loss High, weak sounds /s z f θ/ missed or distorted; voicing errors. Children with cochlear implants made a smaller /s/-/ʃ/ difference than hearing peers (Todd et al. 2011). Listeners need about 9 kHz of bandwidth for child /s/ (Stelmachowicz et al. 2001). Any child with speech errors should have hearing checked.
Motor speech Inconsistent errors, timing problems (Motor speech signs)

Tongue tie. Evidence that ankyloglossia causes r errors, or that release improves speech, is weak: a 2015 systematic review found the data insufficient for non-feeding outcomes (Chinnadurai et al. 2015). A short frenulum alone does not explain an r error, and Speak Up output must never be used to suggest surgery.

Tongue shape for r varies. In 27 adults, 2 used only retroflex r, 16 only bunched and 9 both (Mielke et al. 2016). Judge the sound, not the shape.

sections.title: Treatment context: what the screen can support
sections.body_html:
Speak Up is a screening tool, not a treatment tool, but SLPs ask how the display relates to therapy.

  • Traditional and motor-based treatment: establishment, generalization, maintenance (ASHA), drawing on motor learning principles (practice amount, variability, feedback type and frequency).
  • Visual-acoustic biofeedback: the child sees a live LPC spectrum and tries to bring F3 toward F2. McAllister Byun (2017): 7 children 9 to 15; 3 of 7 showed a significant difference favouring biofeedback. Peterson et al. (2022), telepractice with the staRt app: all 4 children responded to the package, 1 showed a biofeedback advantage.
  • Ultrasound biofeedback: Sugden et al. (2019) review: “may be an effective adjunct”; Yiu et al. (2026) meta-analysis: pooled effect 1.32 with very high heterogeneity and possible publication bias.
  • Randomised trial (C-RESULTS): 108 children 9 to 15; faster progress with biofeedback than motor-based treatment alone (McAllister et al. 2026) and greater generalization (Preston et al. 2026). Exact effect sizes UNVERIFIED (abstracts report significance only).
  • AI-assisted practice: ChainingAI, 5 participants 10 to 19; all 5 generalized pre to post; classifier agreement within the human range for 4 of 5 (Benway and Preston 2024).

On the Speak Up screen: the F3-F2 gap and the spectrum at the cursor show the same dimension visual-acoustic biofeedback trains, which helps explain what changed between tries. The display is not designed or validated as live biofeedback.

sections.title: Limits and cautions
sections.body_html: What can go wrong between the child’s mouth and the number on the screen, and how far to trust the app and its scoring.

sections.title: Microphone distance and placement
sections.body_html:
• Level changes about 6 dB per doubling of distance, so moving the device changes intensity with no change in the child.
  • Close placement improves the signal but risks breath noise and pops (low bursts on the picture). Research setups fix the distance, for example 15 cm from the mouth (Milenkovic et al. 2020).
  • Keep distance and angle the same across sessions if you will compare recordings.

sections.title: Room noise, other voices and reverberation
sections.body_html:
• Steady noise (fans, heating, computers) makes a grey haze, often low, and raises the floor of the 50 dB picture, hiding weak formants such as F3.
  • Other voices add their own harmonics and formants that the tracker may follow. A pitch line in the adult range means an adult voice is in the clip: move the word box or re-record.
  • Echo smears energy forward in time, blurring word ends and stop gaps.

sections.title: Clipping and gain
sections.body_html: A clipped recording (flat-topped waveform) cannot be repaired: it adds energy that is not in the child’s speech. Set the input so the loudest syllables peak well below full scale; the measures table counts clipped samples.

sections.title: Every number is an estimate
sections.body_html: Each formant dot is the output of a model fitted to a short frame and chosen by a tracker. Its accuracy depends on F0, voice quality, noise, nasality (which can interfere with vowel formants, Vorperian and Kent 2007) and how close neighbouring formants are. Even adults’ formants vary: about 60 Hz SD for F1 and 100 Hz for F2 and F3 in men’s vowel imitations (Kent and Forner 1979). Treat a single frame’s value in a high-pitched child as approximate to within about one harmonic spacing (a common working rule, UNVERIFIED as a measured bound), and prefer averages over a stable stretch.

sections.title: Norms and their limits
sections.body_html:
Children’s formants are higher than adults’ and change as they grow; boys and girls diverge around puberty. A gap that is small for a 10-year-old boy may be ordinary for a 5-year-old girl.

  • The r norms most used (Lee et al. 1999, through Flipsen et al. 2001) have 9 to 25 children per age and sex cell, from one region, measured only on “bird” (Campbell et al. 2018).
  • Age-and-sex normalization improved automatic r classification (Benway et al. 2024), but did not remove age and sex effects on SLP ratings (Campbell et al. 2018).
  • Vowel tables for children start at 10 to 12 (Hillenbrand et al. 1995); younger children’s values are higher and not in a checked table.

Practical rules. A raw gap cannot be compared across ages and sexes. Know which sample a “typical range” comes from and whether it matches the word position. Speak Up does not record sex, so its ranges merge boys and girls, which widens them. “No reliable range for this age” is the honest answer when no checked study covers the child.

sections.title: Compare the child with themselves
sections.body_html:
The most robust comparison holds the child’s size, pitch, microphone and room constant:

  1. Record several words with the target, including some likely to be correct (for r, often the vowel in “bird” or r after a velar) and some likely wrong.
  2. Compare the good-sounding tokens with the poor ones, same position, same word if possible.
  3. If no token is correct, compare with the child’s own non-target sounds: for r, F3 in a correct r is roughly two-thirds of the child’s ordinary vowel F3 (60 to 80% in adults, Hagiwara 1995; 0.64 to 0.70 in the vowel data sets, computed for this book). For /s/, compare with the child’s own /ʃ/.

Personalizing an r classifier to the speaker also improved it (Benway et al. 2024), consistent with this advice. Use two cursors to read the two moments side by side.

sections.title: What the F3-F2 gap can and cannot tell you
sections.body_html:
It helps. Normalised F3-F2 was the best of the measures tried for predicting SLP ratings of 6 to 11 year olds (Campbell et al. 2018), and crowd ratings correlated about -0.74 with it (Harel et al. 2017).

It has limits. In 3 to 4 year olds, automatic F3-F2 explained only about 37% of listener ratings (Ancel et al. 2023): about two thirds of what listeners heard was not in the number. Next to /i ɪ j/ the gap is narrow for the wrong reason. A tracker swap makes it meaningless.

Measure at the right point. Research measures at the lowest F3 inside the r, with the analysis settings checked per child (Campbell et al. 2018). Check that the dots sit on bands and that the spectrum shows two peaks before using the number.

sections.title: Arti's limits
sections.body_html:
Arti is a small network trained on the PERCEPT-R corpus to score r as right or wrong.

The corpus. Open American English child and clinical speech for r classification: about 280 speakers aged 6 and up, mostly residual r errors plus typical peers, recruited in New York and New Jersey, mostly lab recordings with headset or lavalier microphones at 44.1 kHz. Labels are listener ratings of the r (“fully rhotic” against “derhotic”, averaged; 0.66 threshold), not transcriptions (Benway et al. 2022; PhonBank).

What published classifiers on this corpus achieved. About .81 F1 for unseen speakers in the lab, personalized (Benway et al. 2023); lower in prospective clinical use (about .57 to .61 against humans, whose own agreement was about .66; Benway and Preston 2023).

Limits for Speak Up:

  1. Age. No published results below 6; Speak Up’s youngest children are outside the data.
  2. Dialect. New York and New Jersey American English; other dialects untested. Expect a non-rhotic r to be called incorrect.
  3. Adult voices. A clip with your model or a background adult may score the wrong voice.
  4. Recording. Lab microphones against a board microphone in a classroom.
  5. Binary only. It cannot say gliding, distortion or omission.
  6. In-between tokens. Humans disagree on them; so will a model trained on humans.
  7. Arti is not the published classifier. Its architecture and accuracy differ; do not quote published numbers as Arti’s accuracy.

Your judgment stands. Note disagreements.

sections.title: How reliable are listeners?
sections.body_html:
• Research treats three trained raters with at least 80% pairwise agreement as a minimum (Campbell et al. 2018, citing McAllister Byun et al. 2015).
  • Bootstrapped groups of 9 naive crowd listeners matched three trained listeners (McAllister Byun et al. 2015).
  • Agreement is lower for in-between (“close”) productions (Klein et al. 2012, direction from the abstract).
  • In prospective clinical use, human-human agreement on r was only moderate (Benway and Preston 2023).

When unsure: listen again later, listen before looking at Arti’s answer, or ask a colleague for a blind second opinion.

sections.title: Screening is not diagnosis
sections.body_html:
A screen sorts children into no concern, monitor and rescreen, or refer for full assessment (ASHA).

Term Meaning here
Sensitivity Of children who truly have a disorder, the share flagged. Low means missed children
Specificity Of children without a disorder, the share passed. Low means over-referral, including dialect speakers and children still learning
Positive predictive value Of flagged children, the share who truly have a disorder. Falls when the condition is rare in the screened group
Base rate About 3.6% persistent disorder at 8 (Wren et al. 2016); far more normal r errors at 4 to 6

Published sensitivity and specificity for automatic r screening of 4 to 12 year olds in schools were not found; Arti’s values on Speak Up’s children are UNVERIFIED unless Speak Up publishes its own check.

sections.title: Recordings and privacy in schools
sections.body_html: Under FERPA, a recording directly related to a student and kept by the school can be an education record (US Department of Education FAQ on photos and videos). Follow district consent procedures, keep recordings on the device or district-approved storage, label with the minimum identifying information, set a retention and deletion schedule, and never upload recordings or share them for model training without explicit permission and district approval. Speak Up’s offline design helps but does not by itself make storage and access compliant. This is not legal advice.

sections.title: If you see this, consider that
sections.body_html:
Aids to listening, not diagnoses. Every row assumes you listened first. “High” and “low” mean compared with the same child’s other tokens.

If you see Consider Then

F3 dips part way, less than the child’s good tokens Distortion, or a close production Use a 3-way judgment; compare with the best token
F3 low only briefly, or late Mistimed r gesture, or a normal fast onset r Check position; compare with /ɝ/; note variability
Low F3 in “bird” but high in “red” Position-specific pattern Report by position
No F3 fall in “car” but good onset r Non-rhotic dialect, or postvocalic deletion Check dialect before scoring
A very brief break, or a few quick pulses at the r Tap or trill Likely second-language influence
Clear F3 dip but the r still sounds wrong Tracker error, or a problem F3 does not capture Trust your ear; look at the bands
F3 dots jump between two bands Tracking error Do not use the gap number
/s/ peak clearly inside 0 to 6 kHz in a child Lowered /s/ (palatal, lateral, rounded context) Compare with the child’s /ʃ/
Gap and burst where a fricative should be Stopping Check age
No formants, very quiet, flat waveform Recording problem or wrong box Re-record; do not score
Flat-topped waveform Clipping Re-record
Pitch in the adult range An adult voice in the box Move the box or re-record
Arti says incorrect, you hear correct (or the reverse) Model error, dialect, recording, in-between token Your judgment stands; note it
Different tracks and error types across repeats of one word Possible motor speech involvement Not diagnosable from the screen; consider referral

sections.title: Glossary
sections.body_html:
Term Meaning
A1-P0 Amplitude of the F1 peak minus the nasal peak; drops in nasalized vowels (Nasal coupling)
Affricate A stop released into a fricative, as /tʃ dʒ/
Antiformant (zero) A frequency where energy is cancelled, from a side branch such as the closed mouth in nasals or the side channels in /l/
Approximant A vowel-like consonant with a narrowing too wide to make noise: /r w l j/
Aspiration Breathy noise after the burst of /p t k/ before voicing starts
Burst The brief noise spike when a stop closure opens
Centroid (M1) The centre of gravity of a noise spectrum
Closure The silent (or voice-bar) stretch while a stop is sealed
Coarticulation Overlap of neighbouring sounds’ movements
Covert contrast A real acoustic difference between two sounds that listeners hear as the same
dBFS Decibels relative to the largest value the recording can hold
Derhotacized An r with too little r-colour
F0 Fundamental frequency, the rate of vocal fold vibration, heard as pitch
F1, F2, F3 First, second and third formants
F3-F2 gap F3 minus F2; small in a good r
Formant A resonance of the throat and mouth; a dark band on the spectrogram
Formant transition A formant sliding between two sounds
Fricative A sound made with turbulent noise through a narrow gap
Gliding Replacing /r/ or /l/ with [w] or [j]
Harmonic A whole-number multiple of F0
Hypernasality Too much nasal resonance on oral sounds
Hyponasality Too little nasal resonance on nasal sounds
Locus The frequency F2 transitions point to for a given place
LPC Linear prediction: the method that estimates formants
Murmur The low, voiced sound of a nasal consonant
Nasal emission Air escaping through the nose on pressure consonants
Narrowband A long-window spectrogram that shows harmonics as lines
Normalization Removing the effect of speaker size so speakers can be compared
Nyquist frequency Half the sample rate; nothing above it is recorded
Perturbation theory How narrowing the tract at different points raises or lowers each formant
Pre-emphasis A filter that boosts high frequencies before analysis
Rhotic Having r-colour; a rhotic dialect pronounces r after vowels
Sibilant A loud, high fricative: /s z ʃ ʒ/
Spectral moments Mean, spread, skew and peakedness of a noise spectrum
Spectrogram Picture of energy by time and frequency
Stop (plosive) A sound with a complete closure and release: /p b t d k g/
Velar pinch F2 and F3 starting close together next to /k g ŋ/
Voice bar Low voicing energy during a closure
VOT Voice onset time: burst to first vocal fold pulse
Wideband A short-window spectrogram that shows formants as bands
z-score How many standard deviations a value is from a group mean
